The committee did not take into account at all the question of prospective dependents, such, for instance, as the case of a widow who was educating her son and spending possibly the savings of her husband's lifetime, or his insurance money, in order to give the boy the advantage of a proper education. In the drafting of this report the committee laid down as a condition precedent to the granting of a pension to a dependent, as distinguished from a pension to a wife who receives pension as of right, that it was only granted where the mother or other dependent was wholly or mainly dependent on the deceased soldier. If the legislation had conie to the House this year, that is one of the aspects of the question which would have required very careful consideration,

and iir my judgment the House would have had to decide what policy should be pursued in relation to this prospective dependency. It is a most serious question, and it comes back to the point raised by my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) in regard to insurance, as to whether or not it was advisable that something should be done by which a compulsory insurance might be put into effect so that there would be something available for those who were left in the event of the man being killed. In my judgment, the committee failed to make provision for just the class of oases to which my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has directed attention, and which in many instances have resulted in great hardship throughout the country.

It seems there is some difficulty in getting a' pension for this woman, because her son had a predisposition to tuberculosis. Supposing that under the literal interpretation of the recommendations of the committee last year, this woman would not he entitled to compensation I sill think that the business of a judge is to render justice and not merely to interpret the law. His interpretation. I still think that the business of a ing justice, and I think, much more than in the case of the judge, the business of the commission is to render justice and not merely to interpret the law. However, I wish to say that without prejudice. I am merely taking a position which I think is in accord with the general view of the people of the country.
There is another point that this committee raises that will have a serious hearing, particularly when compulsory service is instituted. It is a very serious matter. We have found serious cases under the voluntary system, and they will be very much more serious, I am afraid, under the compulsory .system. These are cases where people have financial obligations, and they have no means of carrying them when they have no resources other than the pension. I will give a few instances. I am quite aware that they are outside of the ordinary matter of pensions. We have never considered these cases as being entitled to pen, sions, but in Great Britain, under the Compulsory Service Act, they are taking into account .such cases as these. Under our proposed Compulsory Service Act we will also be warranted in taking note of such cases as the following:

Hannah Lord.-This woman's pension is $32 per month. Previous to the enlistment of her husband, they purchased a lot for $600 upon which $400 has been paid. Interest and taxes for two years are still unpaid.
Amy Bloomer.-This woman's pension is $34 per month. Previous to the enlistment of the soldier they purchased a lot for $2,400, upon which they erected a store and bam for $2,600. There is a mortgage against this property for $2,000, interest overdue $95, taxes about $94. There is no income from this property at present, nor will there be any until times "piclo up" in this city. The total income of this widow is $50,'including the pension. The $16 per month will be reduced as years go by. The widow stated to our committee that unless some help could be obtained until times get good again, she will lose her equity in this property.
Mary E. Marsden.-This woman's pension is $56 per month. She owns a house and lot valued at $5,000 against which there is a mortgage of $1,200. The widow states that she can just live on the pension she receives, and can pay the taxes after severe sacrifices, 'but cannot see how it is possible to redeem the property before foreclosure.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What has been urged by my hon. friend will be taken into consideration by the -Government. It seems rather particularly relevant to the cases of men who enlist under compulsory service. My hon. friend says that the question has been taken up and. dealt with in England under their Oompuls-ory Service Act.
I understand so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I shall have an examination made as to what has been done in Great Britain in that Tegard for the purpose of assisting us in arriving -at a reasonable and fair conclusion as to what could be done along the same lines in this country.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

For the purpose of calling attention to the matters that were brought forward by the Citizens' Committee at Edmonton, I will read a statement of the classes into which these oases are divided.
Class "A"-Cases where the soldier's widow has property encumbered or mortgaged and is unaible to discharge the indebtedness from savings from Pension Fund allowance.
Class "B"-Cases where pension is insufficient at the present time with regard to the high cost of living.
Class "C"-Cases where no pension has been granted owing to strict interpretation of the pension regulations.
These are the three classes of cases which I have already placed before the House,
-and in regard to which there has been some measure of discussion. I wish to instance another case which came under my notice, not in regard 'to pensions, but in connection with the administration of the Patriotic Fund-and I .allude to it merely to establish the fact .that a very serious situation may arise in regard .to the equities in encumbered property when the Military Service Bill is put into force. The case I refer to is that of a woman whose husband volunteered early in the war. They had a house and lot assessed at $6,000 upon which there was a mortgage of $2,500 The mortgage matured, subsequent to the man's enlistment. The mortgagees foreclosed and claimed possession of the property. The soldier's wife contested the action and retained possession by occupation. The matter came to. my attention through the fact that the woman was a claimant on the Patriotic Fund, and her Patriotic Fund allowance was withheld, to either be diverted or to compel her to pay rental to the mortgagees. I bring that instance before the committee, not to discuss the administration of the Fund, but to show how -such cases may arise-where a man not only suffers the ordinary disabilities incidental to serving his country instead of serving himself, but is penalized in large amounts. This case is not one of pension at the present time. But if the man had been killed the woman would have lost not only her support but her property because of the patriotic service rendered by her husband.

The case my hon. friend mentions is one that is not peculiar to his own community. There has been a considerable number of these cases in the West, and my little investigation -at a distance by correspondence leads me to believe there is in these cases no greater hardship-outside of casualties in the field- than that endured by those who remain at home, owing to conditions following upon real estate in western Canada having assumed its present aspect. I should like to know to what conclusion my hon. friend's investigation leads him.

Before six o'clock 1
read the recommendation of the Edmonton .Citizens' Committee, forwarded by the Hon. A. C. Rutherford, and 1 made the suggestion, of which the Prime Minister approved, that the same condition is found to exist in England under the Compulsory Military Service Act and that they are taking some means to minimize the hardship. I do not know what means



they are taking, or how far they are carrying it. I think the proposition is that the Government shall assume ithe responsibility up to a certain limited amount.

These are cases
of compulsory service.

I was alluding to ithis on account of the 'Military Service Act coming into force. I think that we as a country should not give less consideration, tout if possible even imore consideration, to those who are called up than to those who volunteered freely, it is hard to make such a statement, but I think that proposition is fair.
They would pToto-aibly, having regard to the terms of the regulation he exempt here when they would not in England.

That may be. I thought it was only right to draiw attention to this fact, and /to urge, as Ithe committee at Edmonton has urged', that the cases that have already occurred /under voluntary service should receive such consideration /as is within the scope and possibilities of the Government. There is another resolution of this committee that I desire to place before the House. It reads:
That the pension of a widowed mother be the same as that of a wife, provided her son or sons who has or have been killed in action or died on active service were at the time of enlistment or subsequently thereto her sole support.	[DOT]
I do not know how far this goes beyond the present regulation, tout I have read it for the purpose of putting it before the Government.

The question of pensions is a very important one, and no matter what policy Parliament 'adopts that policy will not toe easily carried out. There must of necessity toe cases of injustice at some points. /It ought to toe, and I 'believe it is, the policy of Parliament and of the Government to render these cases just as few and far between as possible. The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) and the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), I think, made some reference this afternoon to insurance.
If I am rightly informed, the men who are to he called upon under the Military Service Act will not be in as good a position as the men overseas have been in the matter of protecting themselves by insurance.
1 was informed yesterday that several of the leading life insurance companies had

instructed their agents to solicit no more insurance on single men, or widowers with families, who were between the ages of the first class to be called. In other words, the insurance companies do not propose to take any risks upon the first 100,000 men who will he called up. It is quite probable that if the required number of men is not secured by the first call, the same attitude will be taken by the insurance companies in reference to the men liable to service in the next draft. This may have something to do with the question of pensions, because the men drafted will not be in as good a position to protect those whom they are leaving behind, no matter what means they have, as were those who have already gone over. Previously, policyholders were at liberty after the expiration of three years, to go wherever they liked; their taking part in the war had no effect upon the amount of their premium. Those who enlisted later had to pay a larger premium or have their policies cancelled. The fact that the insurance companies have asked their agents not to accept any more applications from men between the ages-
That is not universal, is it?

I do not know; this information came to me yesterday. This condition- will make it all the harder for those who go to protect those whom they leave behind, and it will impose upon the State a greater burden and a greater responsibility.
They are endeavouring to select for military service unmarried men in preference to married men.

I am speaking of unmarried men liable to call under the first class, and widowers without families, between the ages of 20 and 34. I wish the member for Kingston to answer two questions. First, when a man reverts in rank, will his family, if the occasion arises, receive pension on the basis of the rank that he held when he left Canada, or on the basis of the lower rank subsequently assumed? Second, what is the position of men, so far as pension is concerned, who, having enlisted with -the Canadian Expeditionary Forces, subsequently became attached to the British forces? .Will they have to rely upon the British Act in the matter of pensions?
The British Act.

I would not wish to delay the committee longer on the -subject, -and I quite appreciate the -spirit in which the minister [DOT](*Mr. Reid) has spoken. As he says, we are all desirous of -seeing that -these men receive -their rights according to the wishes of the people of Canada. At the present time, however, we are not working under an Act of Parliament; we are working under an Order in Council that is oap-able of amendment at the discretion- and on the responsibility of the Government. So, if we consider the enactment not to be final, we are in a better position to-day to meet new -and unforeseen circumstances by amending the Order in Council, than we would be if we were working under an Act of Parliament. I would respectfully suggest that that fact might be taken into consideration, and that where there is found to be a class of cases- not provided for under -the present Order in Council, an amendment might be made to it in order that justice might be done. I would not, for one moment, wish that the Board of Pension Commissioners should not look into every case very carefully. I fully appreciate the fact that they have a responsibility to discharge towards the country in protecting the public moneys, but my complaint wasr-and I am going to take the liberty of repeating i-t-that their -attitude is that they are rather the guardians of the treasury than the champions of the disabled soldiers. My point is that their m-ain duty is the championship of the rights of

the soldiers. The protection of the treasury is part of their duty, but it is rather the second than the first duty. The Board of Pension Commisioners should create a sympathetic .atmosphere in and through their administration, so that the disabled soldier and his ftiends would feel (that, instead of his having to go up against opposition, he was appealing to friends who were making it their business to see that he got justice. I know it is not possible to please every one. I know there are people who make improper claims. I quite appreciate the difficulties that any Board of Pension Commissioners must encounter. But I make the straight and plain criticism that I do not think there has been created that atmosphere of sympathy with the soldier that would lead to more satisfactory administration, and that in the end would work out very much better for the country.

I am sorry I did not have the opportunity of being in the House earlier in the afternoon when this matter was under consideration. I had the honour of being a member of the committee which considered the question of pensions last year, and I recall that the feeling of the committee was that in regard to a great many question we were necessarily working in the dark, and that it was necessary that there should be a revision during the present session of Parliament of the recommendations which we made. I notice that the Minister of Finance has had on the Order Paper since June 11 a resolution which apparently he intended to move, to provide for the revision which we expected last year would take place. A great many questions came before the committee on which it was felt that we could not pronounce with any finality. We felt that a year's experience in working out the problems that arose, together with the experience of the members in regard to their constituents, would help in perfecting an Act this year.
I also desire to recall that it was unanimously agreed by the committee that the men who were to compose the Pensions Board should be chosen after consultation with the leader of the Opposition. That understanding was embodied in the first report presented to the House. But at the request of the Chairman of the Committee, the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), it was agreed that as the terms of the report were to form part of an Order in Council, that recommendation should not be made, it being understood, however, that in accordance with the wishes of the committee the idea would be carried out. I regret to say that the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) did not carry it out, though I personally called his attention to the matter in a letter I addressed to him, and although the fact of this understanding having been arrived at was stated in the House when the matter was under discussion on the very

day 'the House adjourned last session. I think it would have been very much better if the Prime Minister had carried out the idea. The Pension Board ought to be composed of men, and administered under conditions entirely free from political influence. The suggestion 'that there would be any politics in connection with the administration of the pensions regulations would only be an injury to the Government responsible for carrying them out. I have no hesitation in saying that I regard the Prime Minister as not having carried out Iws word on this subject. As I have already said, the statement that this understanding had been arrived at was made in his presence at end of last session; and where a thing of that 'kind is done by common consent all parties should .show good faith in the matter.
I have no fault to find with the personnel of the commission. I think that the gentlemen who compose it have approached the consideration of the problems before them with the highest possible ideals, .and with a v desire .to render the best public service. But I cannot help regarding it as most regrettable that the intention of the committee, as expressed, was not carried out, and that the commission, which might have been composed practically as it is no.w, was not appointed in accordance with that understanding. My hon. friends who were members of that committee will recall that what il am stating in that particular is absolutely correct.
I think it is unfortunate that the Government did not submit the pensions regulations for revision at this session of Parliament. I charge the Government with being negligent in their duty in permitting this motion to stand dn the Order Paper for over three months without calling in the aid of the Pensions Board and the services of the committee which sat last year, or some other committee of Parliament which had given some study to the question.
The Canadian Northern was more important.

My bon. friend says the Canadian Northern was more important. I do not think it was. I think that the proper regulation of pension matters is of the very greatest importance to the people of this country. I think that tlie whole terms of the Order in Council and the report of the committee that was made last year could well have been revised in the light of the experience we have all had in the meantime. The thousand complexities which human nature presents in the ordinary affairs of life do not begin to indicate the tremendous problems with which I have come in contact in my experience with the men of my own constituency who have gone to the front, .and in regard to their friends at home who have been bereaved. Problems have arisen which I had no conception of when, as a member of the committee, I studied this question last year.
This whole question of pensions is wrapped up with the question of the treatment of the men who have gone overseas, and theii conditions of service. I think Canada is paying the hoys at the front entirely too little money; I think wc should pay them .more. I think the Government should have taken up long ago the question of insuring the men who go to the front. That problem ought to be taken into consideration in working out the details of any pension scheme. Apparently, in regard to both these problems the Government is prepared to let matters remain as they are. In comparison with the United States, which has organized in a splendid way in every department that is necessary to maintain their position in the war, this Government shows in a very poor light, in whatever branch of the war you care to mention. The policy of this Government has been haphazard from the beginning. "Anything for the moment," has been its policy.
That is a real scold.

My hon. friend need not worry. He is one of those seraphic beings who could not say anything no matter what the Government did. I would point out that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House who have criticised the Government in the matter of pensions are simply carrying out the suggestion which the minister made a short time ago, when he said that this Government would not know what to do unless they had some criticism in order to help them along the right path. I am, therefore, performing a duty in the interests of the Government. I say that it is a scandal that this whole question of pensions should have been allowed to stand as it is. My hon. friend intimates that there is going to be an Order in Council to increase the pensions. That should have been a matter for consideration by hon. members of this House, and for a committee of this House, entirely apart from any question of party.
There is another matter. With reference to the rules incorporated in the Order in

Counoil, I think we should have given, and should give now, to the Pensions Board, wider discretion in regard to the numerous cases which are liable to arise and which will prove exceptions to the general rules we laid down. I have in mind one or two instances. A father whose boy has been killed at the front, or has died as the result of injuries received or disease contracted or aggravated while on active service, is entitled to a pension .in class 3.
I have in mind the case of a poor old workingman in my county. Two of his elder sons were married. One of the younger boys upon whom he largely depended for getting along worked in one of the industries nearby. This boy went to the front and was killed. The man's wife died in the meantime. His second son volunteered and went to the front, and the younger boy did not give his father half of his pay. The result is, the old man is practically destitute. Under the conditions and rules which have been laid down, the Pension Board cannot see its way clear to give him anything. This is an instance in which the pension commissioners ought to have wider discretion, and if the opportunity had been afforded us to deal in review with the regulations which were laid down last year, I would have urged, if I had been on the committee, ithat wider discretionary power should be given to the commission to deal with such cases. Another case is that of a widowed mother, one of whose boys went to the front and was killed. Her husband died in the meantime. She has another son, sixteen years old, who is not much good. She is in receipt of a pension under the regulations, which will cease the moment that boy reaches the age of .seventeen or eighteen, and he will probably turn out to be no good whatever. This poor woman is bereft of the one who might have been able to help her, and under the regulations she is cut off from receiving any pension. If wider discretion were left with the board to deal with cases of this kind, undoubtedly she would be looked after. Let me give still, another case. A man who had been through the South African war volunteered for service overseas. While training in Halifax he was thrown and broke his kneecap. Of course it was impossible for him to go overseas. He was allowed a pension and he still walks lame, and will be lame for the rest of his life. Before he enlisted he was a coal miner, and of course it is impossible for him to engage in coal mining again.
Was he injured on this side of the Atlantic?

Yes, but he was in the overseas forces, .and he would have been entitled to a pension, so that the case comes within the purport *of these regulations. While the shell manufacturing was going on he got .some work in that industry, but this is now stopped. I received a letter from him the other day in which he tells me that on the principle of bad luck never coming singly, he has received word from the Pension Board to the effect that, basing themselves upon some medical report, he is not to receive any more pension. I have no do.ubt .the Pension Board is dealing with this case in accordance with the regulations. I intend to call upon the board for the purpose of giving this man's name, and the full particulars. The net result of the whole thing is that he is lame for life and cannot engage in his usual occupation, and his pension is being cut off because, I apprehend, the .board is tied down by the letter of the law as incorporated in the Order in Council. The Government are taking full responsibility for this law; they have not consulted Parliament in regard to the matter and apparently have decided that they would not do so. They propose to deal with the question by Order in Council. With all the complexity of the problems that must come before any Parliament in this country, we have allowed a year ,to go by without any revision of those pension regulations. I regard this as very unfortunate. The difficulty will not be met by simply increasing the amount of the pensions. There must be a total revision of these regulations along certain lines, and the Government, with an election upon them and with .all the problems to be dealt with in the next six months, will not be able to give this question the consideration to which it is entitled. I believe the Pension Board is determined to do what is right, and I believe we may safely trust them. At the same time, I regard it as most unfortunate that the Government has allowed a year to elapse without dealing with the problem, and that we are now coming to the end of this Parliament with a law which is practically a year and a half old, without the benefit of the changes suggested by the experience which has been gathered in the time intervening, and that we cannot look for any immediate improvement or change in the law upon a permanent basis or upon such lines that calm deliberation and intelligence and care ap-

plied to the framing of a law would produce.
My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Miaedonald) first complains that in the appointment of this commission he understood the committee had suggested
I did not understand it; I knew it.
My hon. friend says he knew the committee had recommended that the leader of the Opposition should be consulted in the appointment of this commission. This is the first time I have heard of it.

Let me say to my hon. friend that it was stated in Parliament on a motion to adopt the report of the committee. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries moved the adoption of the report last year, and I seconded. If my hon. friend will look at Hansard he will see that my statement is correct.

I do not doubt my hon. friend's statement at all. He also told us he had written a letter to the Prime Minister. This is the first I have heard of it. Probably I was not in the House when the discussion took place. If the Prime Minister Wad that understanding I am quite satisfied he must have overlooked it, and that he had no intention whatever of not fully carrying out any understanding which may have been arrived at. In any event, even if 'a mistake were made so far 'as the understanding is concerned, my hon. friend agrees that the three commissioners who were appointed were men in whom the people of Canada had every confidence. I think that in making the selection the Prime Minister dhose men whom no person would criticise a<s being unfair in the administration of those pension regulations. So far as concerns the submission of the Bill at this session, I may say that the notice on the Order Paper referred to by my hon. friend was simply a notice of a Bill authorizing the appointment of the Board of Commissioners, not of a Bill to establish the rate of pensions. The reason no Bill was submitted this session is that we have not had an opportunity of submitting one. I think every member of this House will agree that we have had most important legislation from the time the Prime Minister came back in May down to the present moment, legislation that had to go through, legislation that could not wait. The financial Bills and the other Bills had to go through; there can be no
doubt about that. Even the Canadian Northern Railway Bill, to which my hon. friend refers, was a Bill which had to go through, otherwise there would be a financial crisis in the country.
It is going to make one anyway.
No, it will not.
It will make a worse crisis than if nothing at all had been done.

No. That Bill had to go through, and the other Bills had to go through, and this session has been kept busy. I believe that in the twenty-six years that I have been here there never has been as much important legislation passed as during the present session.
There never was so much bad legislation.

It is all good legislation. The present pension law is administered in the same way as if it had been a law passed by Parliament. Anything that is necessary to meet the situation or to provide amendments can be done by Order in Council, and the Prime Minister stated that some matters that were brought to his attention to-day, and other matters, were being considered by the Government. Hon. gentlemen will admit that with this House continuously in session, and ministers busy here all day and up to late at night, it was impossible to take many things that were urgent.

You are the only
minister who does any work.

No. they have all been working very hard. This question will be taken up and dealt with and we will carry the matter along until Parliament meets again. The hon. gentleman speaks of what the United States have done in the short time since they have been at war. He knows that when this war came on there was no preparation. We had to initiate everything and get the organization started. The United States knew this war was going on and they were getting ready for the war that they would eventually get into. They have had the advantage of our experience and of that of other nations. I believe that the Government and people of this country have done more in this war than the Government and people of any other country in the world. I do not take second place to any country or government. The people and Government of Canada have done

everything possible to further their participation in the war. The question of an increase in the pensions is being considered ai d an increase will be given. The present rate of pensions was unanimously agreed to bv the members of this House and now all agree that the question of the rate of pensions should again be considered. The Government are considering the matter and will come to a conclusion as to an increase in the pension. When we meet again the House will be in a position to reconsider and readjust the whole matter. A matter of this kind is very important to the men at the front, to those whom they have left behind and to the people of the country as a whole. Criticism with regard to it is good. While the criticism of my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) is very severe, we are still glad to have it. This criticism will result in good and we will consider the different suggestions which have been made.
I was surprised to hear my hon.
9pm friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) say that there was a possibility that he might not return. We all like to have him here.

I presume that is why
my hon. friend insists on putting through the Military Voters' Bill and the War-Time Elections Bill.

I am in thorough sympathy with this vote and I do not wish for a moment to delay its passage. But the minister slid over one or two questions that I did think he ought to have dealt with. On two or three occasions the question of insuring the lives of soldiers was brought up by speakers, and I do not think that the minister has given any answer on that question. It is a matter of the very greatest importance, .and if it is true that the insurance companies have refused altogether to accept risks on the men who are liable to be called out, then ilt is a question upon which the Government ought to take some action. I recollect that at the time of the South African war, the late Right Hon. Sir Charles Tupper proposed a scheme by which the lives of the soldiers were to be protected by life insurance. I do not think his scheme was ever carried out, but I remember that he advocated it. I have seen in the press that in the United States the premium1 of insurance on, a soldier is very low. Something like $3.50 or $4 a month for $5,000 is what is being paid by soldiers who have been recruited under the new Military Service Bill of the United

States. I have no doubt that soime arrangements have been made by the Government of the United States with the insurance companies by which they are protected financially. Why is it that our Government have not done something? Is it not of the greatest importance that the men who can afford to pay life insurance should have an opportunity of insuring their lives before they are drafted? I join with my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) in condemning the Govfernment for having allowed this question of pensions to lie over since the 11th of June, without having dealt with it. Why did they not deal with it? Surely they have had time enough to take this question up since the 11th of June. Look at the resolution placed on the Order Paper by the hon. the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White). I think the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) was a little astray in what he told us to-night. He explained that this proposal was simply for the purpose of appointing a commission and of making certain regulations governing the commission, but that it did not give them any power to deal with the question of pensions. If he looks at the- proposal on the Order Paper he will find that he is altogether mistaken in regard to the effect of it. This is the proposal:
Resolved, that it is expedient to establish a Commission to be known as "The Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada," consisting of three Commissioners, and to provide for salaries and expenses in connection therewith, and to empower the Board to award pensions, allowances, and gratuities to any persons who nave served in the military or naval expeditionary forces of Canada during the present war and have been disabled on such service, and to their children; and to the widows, children and dependents of such persons when death occurs during or was due to such service; the said pensions, allowances and gratuities to be paid out of moneys appropriated by Parliament for the purpose.
You will see that the resolution deals not only with the appointment of a pension commission, but with the whole question of pensions. There is no doubt that the Government deserves to he condemned for neglecting this important matter all through last summer. It should have been dealt with. There are a number of other things in connection with the military affairs of this country on which the Government has fallen, down and with which it has not dealt. It has fallen down on the question of national service; on the question of recruiting; on the question of raising the soldiers'	paywhich has been brought up in the

House a number of times-on the question of pensions, and has devoted all its time for the last (few months to schemes of a very low order, tampering rwith the franchise, as any one can see by the measure now being forced through the Senate. The Government has had plenty of time to attend to questions of that kind, but apparently not time to attend to important questions in relation to our military forces, which should have been attended to. What has the minister to say about the insurance policies?

The hon. member for Edmonton raised the insurance question this afternoon. He referred to the fact that it had been brought to the attention of the Government and the Prime Minister informed him that the whole matter would be taken into consideration.

It seems to me a regrettable fact that great hardships have arisen, and will arise in the future, in regard to pensions, unless the Government takes steps to put the law on a better basis. I have at this moment received an answer to an application for a pension from a widow in my county. The case seems to me a very hard one indeed. As the hon. member for Piotou was speaking I was reading the letter I received from the Board of Pension Commissioners refusing the application for the pension. The situation is this: Some fifteen years ago this woman was left a widow with six young children. She had a small farm and kept her family together until they grew up. One married, and two sons were left at home. One enlisted and went to the front, returned and was discharged. After he recovered his health he re-enlisted and went overseas the second time. He had been there only a few" months when he was killed. The eldest son is at home working the farm, but he may leave at any time and get married, or anything may happen to him, and if anything happens, this widow will be absolutely alone. The board refused the pension, and they were probably right according to law. I have no fault to find with the Board of Pension Commissioners, I have had occasion to go to the board during the last two or three years and have been treated with the greatest courtesy, and I think they would do the best they could under the circumstances. The answer I have received from them to-night is that the law reads " wholly or mainly dependent upon;" and, they cannot get around that point. They practically .admit, although they do not say it in so many words, that it is a hardship. Reading between the lines, I would say they -consider the case one in which relief should be given. 'This woman is ipoor. Her son has given his life in defence of his country. And now, because of some words in the la/w, the com- . missioners are debarred from considering the question of granting the pension which she deserves, and which I am suro the commissioners think she deserves. If such is the law-and I presume it is-it is very unfortunate that Parliament is to be prorogued without placing upon the statute-book a law giving greater latitude to the commissioners, permitting them to investigate each particular case, and -deal with each case on -its merits. This case, I am sure, deserves the greatest consideration. I understand the Minister of Customs, who has charge of these estimates, to state that while no law is being passed this year to amend the Pensions Act, these cases will be provided for by Order in Council. I sincerely trust such an Order may be passed as will give relief in this and other cases on the same footing.
Pensions payable to militiamen and on active service as follows:	Northwest Rebellion, 1S85,
$14,000 ; general, $30,000.
The -hon. member for Edmonton wanted a list of those receiving pensions under the item " Northwest Rebellion, 1885."
No, I did not wish for that. All I wanted was to know how it came that we were voting this particular sum of money for the Northwest rebellion.
We pay it every year to the Northwest Rebellion veterans.
Is- it- not different from the item last year?
No, it is the old item. We have it every year. The whole list is in the Auditor General's Report. The question was as to the militia pensions generally.

I understood the minister to say that part of this .money was for the Home Defence, or Home Guard Service. I desire a fuller explanation in regard to that. Besides, there is an increase of $24,000 since last year. That is what particularly claimed my attention.

The hon. gentleman will remember the letter I read from the Militia Department, in which it was said that the increase was on account of men. on the

Home Defence. There is one general 'pension account as it were. On account of the large number of men serving in the Home Defence force, the pension list is increasing. For instance, a member of the Home Defence force, while guarding one of the locks, was killed through no fault of nis own. His case would come under the Militia Act.

The item shows an increase of $24,000, which, I assume, is entirely in respect of pensions on account of disability during service in the home defence force. The size or extent of the home defence force, the circumstances under which it is maintained, and the kind of service it renders, are things which are not generally known." What are the circumstances that call for this extra payment of pensions? Is the scale of pensions in this case the same as that provided in the case of overseas service, or is it the old scale that prevailed some years ago?
The old scale.

Militia pensions generally are for all those in the militia engaged in active service, but not overseas. A great number of men' have been employed in guarding canals, elevators, railways, bridges, public buildings, and so on. Accidents are bound to occur among these men, and the pension list accordingly increases. These pensions are dealt with as they have been for some years, by the Militia Council on the old scale. I think that a return was brought down giving the information asked for by my hon. friend up to a certain date. The only information that it would be necessary for me to furnish in response to his request is that covering the period since the bringing down of that return.

I do not insist upon that. Rut what I find strange is that in this home defence force there should be an increase in one year of $24,000 for pensions. The war has been going on for three years, and it is rather unaccountable that there should be a fourfold increase during the year.

That is information that the hon. gentleman should have. The letter that I read this afternoon from the Paymaster General gave the estimate of the amount required during the fiscal year. Of course, the whole of the amount may not be used, but it is necessary to provide an amount to cover all possible requirements.
My hon. friend told us this afternoon that this vote was for pensioners under the Militia Act. The pensioners we have under the Militia Act are officers.
No.
Very largely. I know some officers at headquarters who have been pensioned under the Militia Act.

The hon. member is wrong when he .says that only officers are pensioned under the Militia Act. Under the Pay and Allowance regulations which took effect September 1, 1914, it was provided as follows:
The following rates of pensions will he granted militiamen wounded or disabled on active service, during drill or training, or on other military duty, provided the disability was not due to his own fault or negligence.
These regulations provide for pensions to men of the first, second, third and fourth degrees, of the following ranks: rank and file; sergeant; .squad, battery or company or sergeant-major; squad, battery, or company quartermaster-sergeant; colour sergeant; staff sergeant; regimental sergeant-major; master gunner; regimental quartermaster-sergeant; warrant officer-

Those are members
of the permanent force?
No, those are all on active service, and as I have stated, there are many men on home service in this country.
How many?
I do not know, but the return, up to a certain date, has been brought down. I have not the later information. If my hon. friend desires it, I will write to the department for the information.

All we want to know is
how this very remarkable increase in the estimates, in regard to this particular item, comes about. We really ought to have that information because the increase is a very startling one. While I would not wish to be too suspicious, when we see the figures of the estimates performing such startling gymnastics, we necessarily become suspicious.

The hon. member, of course, knows the way in which these pensions to men on active service are dealt with. Every claim for a pension by a militiaman must come before the Militia Council and be passed by them. The Militia Council make a recommandation to Council. The matter then goes before the Treasury Board which

must examine and pass upon the pension, and then it goes before Council in which the matter is taken up. The hon. member, therefore, from his own experience in regard to these matters, will, I think, agree with me that there is not much opportunity for money being improperly expended. I feel, of course, as the Paymaster' General has stated, that he has put in an amount that he would be sure would cover any amount that would be required for any one injured on actiwe service. This includes not only the regular active militia, but the extra men who have been put on or enlisted in the active militia for home guard duty.

Why does the minister not put the whole of the pensions under the one control? There is no use in having these side pensions administered in-this way. There is no reason why they should not be transferred by Order in Council.

These pensions are, as I
have stated, administered by the Militia Council, but they are all paid through the Pensions Board.
Why should they not be altogether under the Pensions Board?
That matter will probably be taken up later on. That Taises the whole question of pensions, and I cannot answer as to the question of policy.

I think I can clear up the matter. The report of the special committee of last year dealt with the question of pensions for members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force. The committee recommended, as the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) will remember, that a commission be appointed to take charge of and administer that particular branch of the pension work. The militia pensions to which the hon. member refers are -not pensions to officers who have retired after long service, but are pensions paid to members of the militia in Canada, such as the home guard, who suffer disability. The hon. gentleman will remember that, when the documents were referred to the committee of last session, there was in effect a -scheme of pensions by which $264 was -granted to members of the rank and file. That scheme of pensions was not affected by the report of the committee in so far as i-t -affected the members of the Canadian Defence Force, the Home Guard, and -so on. The report of the committee dealt only with the members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force. As I understand the practice -at the present time,
the Pensions and Claims Board of the Militia Department determine what pensions shall be paid to members of the Canadian militia, and the payment is then made through the Pensions Board. The whole matter as to the centralization under the one commission rests until legislation is introduced in this House. But the pensions to officers are commonly known as the pensions under the Act of 1901, that is, pensions for long service.

Are those voted
separately, or are they included in the general vote?

They are voted separately,
I understand.
Will the minister -arrange to give us to-morrow a list of the parties who are receiving pensions under this vote?

Yes.
Penitentiaries-To provide a further amount necessary in consequence of the error in item No. 414 of the Supplementary Estimates, for a bonus not exceeding $100 each to penitentiary officials and employees whose salary was $1,000 or less on April 1, 1917, $6,000.

Did not this item
stand for some information?

This item was puit in to
cover an error in the original estimate. ^Provision was- made for the payment of a bonus of $100 to those whose salaries were $1,000 or less. There were in the penitentiaries -about 60 industrial guards who were left out of the count in the -estimate, and this is simply to cover an error in the computation.

Does that apply to all the
penitentiaries- in the Dominion?
It is general in fits -application.

I did not -happen- to be here when the item amounting to $26,500 of which this is a part, was taken up. I am not opposing the increase or bonus of $100 to those guards, although I see no reason why it should be limited to the guards and should not be given to the men on the clerical staff. If you simply regard this matter from the standpoint of the amount of salary paid to the guards in- the penitentiaries, you will not be considering it as it should be considered.
In addition to the -salary of $800 or $900, as the ease may be, every guard receives two -suits o-f clothes, an overcoat, cap, boots, and so on. He is allowed two weeks' holi-

days during the year, -and a gratuity is provided for which is equivalent to -the Government keeping insurance in force, so to speak, to an amount anywhere from $1,200 to $1,800, according -to the length of time the guard has served 'and the salary he has received. For instance, a man drawing $76 a month who had served twenty years would draw on retirement a lump eum of $1,500. Frequently, men have retired and drawn that amount, and then -gone into, some other occupation.
Do they pay anything towards it?

Nothing whatever. I
have in mind the case of a guard who, upon retirement at his own request, drew a gratuity of $1,200 or $1,500-1 forget just which-and was afterwards taken on the staff, although he had been retired. There is really supposed to be only one reason for a man retiring, and that is physical or mental unfitness for .his position. One would naturally suppose, therefore, that if a man retired on account of physical or mental unfitness and drew a gratuity, he would not be replaced on the staff, but there was at least one case where that occurred, and the man ie on the staff at the present time. I do not think -the principle of giving a gratuity to the guard is a right one. I think their salaries ought to be regulated in -some 6uch way as the salaries of civil servants. Giving a gratuity to a man makes him a slave to hie superior officers. Under those conditions a -m-an is afraid to express an opinion lest he incur the displeasure of his superior officer, who might report him in such a way that it would be impossible for him to obtain a gratuity, or perhaps compel him to retire on grounds other than those of ill-health and thereby lose the gratuity which he had earned during his years of service. It does seem to me -that the logical and reasonable thing to- do would be to fix a minimum salary -and then allow a certain amount for good conduct, and let the salary advance to certain maximum. There would then be an incentive to a man to do his best. He would get paid as he went along, -and when he retired -he need receive no gratuity or pension of any kind. When this matter was under discussion before, the Minister of Justice referred to the case of a man who had been employed for a great many years in one of our western, institutions, and who died very suddenly of heart disease. Dying suddenly in that way, without any opportunity of putting in a -claim 
for a gratuity, there was nothing coming to his family, notwithstanding the fact that this man had served for thirty-two years. As the 'Minister of Justice pointed out, that was a case of extreme hardship. The man's family did not have anything to live on, and there was -no gratuity coming to them because the -man had not retired on account of illness. But if twenty-four hours before his death, he bad made up his mind to retire, and had made application accordingly on the ground of ill-health, He would have drawn $1,700 or $1,800. But, being suddenly stricken with heart disease, there was nothing coming to him, unless the government granted a -compassionate allowance. The -case was dealt .with in that way, and very properly, by Parliament. That case seems to me to prove conclusively that the present system is asolutely iPogi-eal and unfair.
I know of a case where a man by the name of Young, who had been a guard for many years, was taken ill. He did not send in his resignation or apply for his retiring allowance because he expected to get better and return to his work. He withheld sending in the necessary papers to Ottawa until (just -a few hours too late. The man died. The papers did not get here in time, and -his family was deprived of an amount which they would (have obtained if the papers had arrived -here a few minutes sooner.
On what basis are gratuities granted? Is so much counted for every year's service ?

Supposing a man's
salary during the -past three years had averaged $75 a month, and he had been employed as a guard for twenty years. Upon retiring he would receive one -month's salary for every year he had served; that is, twenty times $75, or $1,500. I think I have stated it correctly.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
But if he dies, his family gets nothing?

Absolutely nothing,
unless the Government grants a compassionate allowance, as they did in a case -last week. Speaking on that case the Minister of Justice said:	"On inquiry I find that
it is most unlikely that other cases of a similar kind would occur; so that this will not be establishing a precedent." That simply means that the Minister of Justice is under the impression that there will not

be any more guards die of heart disease and thereby be excluded from obtaining the pension they would have received if they had retired in the ordinary way.

You cannot tell that.
Mr. EDM7ARDS: No, I don't think so. However, to return to the matter of the guards and their salaries. In addition to their salaries they get these articles of clothing which I have mentioned, and that is not all. I think I am right in saying that when they are on duty at the prison they have to take some of their meals there. These meals they get at about twelve and a half or thirteen cents each. They also get a great many things from the prison at a much lower price than ordinary people can get them elsewhere. For instance, most excellent bread is made at the prisons, and all the guards have to do is to put in a requisition for whatever bread they want for themselves and their- families, and they get it at several cents a loaf less than the ordinary citizen has to pay. This provision for gratuity is equivalent to a paid-up insurance policy. Taking all these things into consideration, I do not think I am extravagant in saying that you are adding $150 a year to their salaries in the way of these perquisites. The work they perform is not heavy work. True, there is a certain element of danger connected with it, but it is not work which requires very great education, and the salaries of these men are as good as if not better than the salaries of the clerical staff. There are hundreds of employees in the various branches of the public service whose hours are very much longer than those of the penitentiary guards, and whose work is very much more particular, yet they are receiving less salary than those men. It is said this is not an increase in salary, but simply a bonus granted because of the high cost of living at the present time. We may call it a bonus for the time being, but I am satisfied that once they receive this grant it will be very hard to cut it off. The probabilities are that it will never be cut off. I do not wish to be understood as being opposed to the granting of this $100 to them, but I think consideration should also be given to the clerical staff who, in my judgment, are not overpaid.
There are one or two other matters in connection with the penitentiaries to which I would like to call attention. In the first "place there is the lack of suitable prison employments. This was referred to by Mr. Douglas Stewart, Inspector of Penitentiaries, in his reports. He states that this is one of the principal difficulties with which the penitentiary officials have to contend.
I think that difficulty could be largely removed by making use of the services of prisoners to produce many articles which are required in our Government buildings throughout the country, articles of furniture, for instance, and for the manufacture of rural mail boxes, as well as a hundred and one other things that could be mentioned. I know this suggestion will be me: with the old song that we are "competing with free labour." But this is a State institution, maintained at the expense of the State, and the State should have a right to make use of the services of these men to produce such articles as it may require. Some departure has been made from the ordinary routine during the last two or three years. We have made use of prison labour to a certain extent in improving the roads around Kingston. Might I impress upon the minister that I think the convict labour of the Kingston penitentiary might very well be used in rebuilding the piece of road which was taken over by the late Government from Cataraqui bridge up through the military camp. The Government has to maintain this piece of road, and I see no reason why the prisoners could not be employed in maintaining it. There is any amount of material there, but men are scarce. I do not know how this will be received by the minister, but I recommend ;t to his careful consideration.
One of the principal causes of trouble in our penitentiaries at the present time is that the men are not allowed to have tobacco. They get it in an underhand way, and there has been a good deal of difficulty on that account. Guards have been charged with taking money for conveying tobacco to the prisoners. I think one of the best means of putting an end to that trouble would be to allow the convicts a limited supply of tobacco. However, that is a matter upon which opinions may very widelv differ.
*Many years ago Sir John Thompson proposed erecting a penal institution to take care of youthful convicts under twenty years of age. That movement ended with Sir ' John Thompson's death. I think it is a matter that wp might very seriously consider. I notice by the last prison statistics that we have, those for the year ended March 31, 1915, that 187 convicts twenty years of age and under are in our various penal institutions. Some of these might have been serving a second or third term

but I think it very unlikely. I would assume that most of them were in for the first time. I do think that these young men can hardly be expected to leave those institutions any better than when they went in. Suppose they are first offenders, they are brought into contact with old criminals, men who have spent a good part of their lives behind prison walls. I do not think we are giving these young fellows a square deal, a fair show. The object of imprisonment is twofold. A man must be taught that he must expect to be punished if he violates the laws of the land. But surely that is not the sole and only object of sending him to prison. It may be the first thing to consider, fbut we should also consider the possibility of turning that man out at the expiration of his sentence with the prospect of becoming a good and useful citizen. If young lads twenty years of age and under could be sent to a separate institution, located somewhere between Kingston and Montreal, and kept toy themselves, there would toe a better chance of their becoming useful citizens than there is when they are housed with men of all classes as they are at tlhe present time. In that connection, it is very interesting to note that in the Kingston penitentiary 3.7 per cent of the convicts were less than twenty or only 21 out of a total population of 559. At St. Vincent de Paul there were 72 out of a population of 447-over 16 per cent-were under twenty years of age. Dorchester about 141 per cent of the population was under twenty; in Manitoba 121 per cent and in British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan between 5 and 6 per cent. I am not going to undertake to give a reason for that; I frankly admit I cannot give a reason. But the figures arrested my attention. I could not help but note .such a large percentage in St. Vincent de Paul and Dorchester pen-itentaries-16 and 14} per cent as compared with 3.7 per cent at Kingston. That is something for which there may be an explanation but it does not occur to me. The percentage of convicts in various institutions who are put down as intemperate is also worth noting. In this connection Alberta has the best record, less than three per cent of its prison population being put down as 10 p.m. intemperate, while at St. Vincent de Paul the number is 48} per cent, Kingston, 37} per cent; Manitoba, 40 per cent, and British Columbia 6-8 per cent.
I am told that since the passing of prohibition in Ontario and in other provinces 
where prohibitory measures have been passed, a very marked effect has been noticeable upon the prison population, that it is much less than formerly. The lessened number of convicts is attributed to a very large extent to the difficulty people have at the present time in getting liquor. I think possibly that is true.
If I might refer again to the matter which is uppermost in my mind in connection with our penal institutions, I would like to impress upon the Minister of Justice and the members of this House the importance of seriously considering the erection of a separate institution for boys under twenty or twenty-one years of age who are first offenders. I honestly believe that such an institution will more than pay for itself, even if you consider only the matter of dollars and cents. But if you estimate its value upon other lines, the possible reclamation of young men who may become useful citizens, it is impossible to state in terms of money its value to the country. We ought to do all that we possibly can as representatives of the people to reclaim any of those fellows where it is possible to reclaim them. I do not think that there is any man entirely so bad that there is no- good in him, and perhaps we might turn that around and say that there is no man so good hut there is some bad in him. I think there is some good in every man, and you will get it out of him if you go the right way about it. I do not think that a boy who is sent to prison for the first time has a fair show to come out of that institution and become a useful member of society, having to mix, as he does, with criminals of all classes. I believe that as men who are interested in our fellow men we ought seriously to consider, as Sir John Thompson did, the erection of such an institution as I have mentioned to take care of the young men who are found in our various penal institutions. That is the main reason why I rose to speak to-night. I sincerely ask the members of this House to give the matter consideration.

I certainly think a great many of my hon. friend's remarks are very timely, and I rise to endorse what he has said in regard to separate institutions, such as the prison farm, where the younger men who are not steeped in crime can. be given employment. The theory of the present day in reference to prisons is that they are just as much for reformation as for punish-' ment. They have made a marked success at Sing Sing along that line, and certainly

nothing could be more successful than the efforts of the Hon. Mr. Hanna in establishing a prison farm at Guelph. He has had wonderful success in reforming a great many men who were sent to prison. My hon. friend's remarks along that line are very much to the point, and I think the minister will give them .serious consideration.
I desire to ask the minister whether the men working at the penitentiary are paid anything? In many institutions they pay the prisoners a certain amount for their work, and when they go <jut into the world they are not entirely destitute. I understand they give them a suit of clothes when they leave the penitentiary. Advocates of prison reform in the United States lay great stress on the advisability of paying the men something so as to give them a start in the world when they are discharged. Is there any system of that kind in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At present the convict is not paid anything for his work.

I cannot say whether or not the committee has been particularly impressed with what the hon. member for Frontenac has said with reference to wages paid the guards and employees of the Kingston penitentiary. While certainly he did not criticise these employees in so many words, I do not think I would be outside the mark in saying that he almost damned them with faint praise. With reference to the remuneration paid to a man for services, it makes a great deal of difference from what angle you view the subject, and I am rather inclined to think that the hon. gentleman from Frontenac viewed this matter from the point of view of the man who lives in the country, rather than the point of view of the city man. The ordinary guard in the Kingston penitentiary-and I think, similarly, in other penitentiaries in Canada -receives $800 a year. He has to work 305 days and loses practically part of each Sunday. He gets two suits of clothes, a pair of boots, a hat, and other perquisites, and is allowed to take advantage of the bakery and buy bread at cost. When you consider what it costs to live in Canada today, and what the industrial workers outside are getting, I do not think any member of this committee will contend that a man receiving $900 a year-as that is the remuneration of the guard, with $100 added -is being exorbitantly paid for his services. We must have regard from the point of view of the work these men have to undertake. It is a position of great trust, in which a man,
if he is dishonest, can make a great deal of money by trafficking with the convicts. You expect honesty and efficiency, and you expect the guard to keep himself neat and tidy when off duty. Last autumn or early last spring a delegation of the guards came to my house, and some of them explained to me that, living as they could, they were going behind $4 or $5 a month, without meeting clothing expenses of their family or doctor's expenses. I regret, as well as the hon. member for Frontenac, that the clerical staff has not had an increase. They are doing their work well, and many of them are not paid adequately for their services, but the Government laid down the principle that no man in receipt of more than $1,000 salary should receive the bonus, and those oil the clerical staff, being all paid in excess of $1,000, could not take advantage of the regulation. The vote is not limited strictly to the industrial guards, but it is limited to those whose salary does not exceed $1,000. The hon. member for Frontenac has said in one breath that the gratuity system practically amounted to an insurance policy, and in the next breath admitted that it was not an insurance or superannuation, but a gratuity paid to a man, for years of service, who does not resign, but is relieved from service, the man's conduct having been good. If a man dies in the employ of the penitentiary no superannuation is paid to his wife. If he resigns he gets nothing; he severs his connection with the penitentiary, and gets what is coming to him, and that ends it. If he dies in the ordinary course of human affairs, nothing is paid to his widow. It is not an insurance. The Government simply says to the penitentiary guard: " If you do your duty faithfully and well, and if you live beyond the allotted span of life, and become so worn out in the Government service that you are not fit to continue the performance of your duties, then we will give you a gratuity, something to live on, in your declining days. But this provision cannot be taken advantage of by the wife or family of the guard.
I might say-and I think the hon. member for Frontenac will bear me out-that this year the convicts of the Kingston penitentiary have done more than usual of constructive work. They have built a magnificent roadway in front of the penitentiary proper, and partially in the village that lies to the west of the penitentiary. They have done more farm work than usual, because

the cry tor increased production made available land that did not belong (to the penitentiary, but -which, was placed at the 'Government's disposal by the owners, so that a crop might be raised on it this year. I think I am safe in saying that more work has 'been done this year than in former years. But when it comes to the question of turning the convicts over to work in gangs on general road construction, I think the hon. member for Frontenac and I do not see eye to eye. In my judgment the work for the convict should be work of a constructive character, from the point of view of the upbuilding of the convict, the development of habits in him that would be useful; and he should learn a trade. Then, when he leaves the institution, he could turn his knowledge to advantage. I may not be right in my conclusion, but I think that many men return to the penitentiary after having left it because they are not able to earn a decent living outside. I have always thought that if a man left there instructed in a trade so that he could earn a living, he would not drift back into the penitentiary. But if we are going to make it an industrial drudgery, the man is no better when he leaves than when he went into the institution. My idea is that the great work in whicfy these men should be instructed is agriculture. The cry from one end of tlhe country to the other is for assistance on the farm. If, after the w-aT is over and things are more or less settled, the Minister of Justice could see his way to buy large tracts of land adjacent to the several penitentiaries and give the men instructions in scientific agriculture, I think he would take a long step towards solving our penitentiary problems. Many men, if they were instructed as agricultural labourers, would leave the cities and go into the country. They would be in a new environment; they would be removed from their old haunts and from the temptations to which they had previously been subjected. I sincerely trust that this matter will not escape the attention of the Minister of Justice. With regard to tobacco, some people may say that it is a luxury. I have talked with many inmates of penitentiaries, and I know that many of them get tobacco against the rules. It is sent in to them; there is a certain amount of traffic in it. If the men are going to get it; if they are willing to break the rules to obtain it, it seems to me that it would not be unwise for the Government to make some provision by which the men could get a definite 
allowance of tobacco as a reward for good conduct and faithfulness or service. Some of the men. tell me that the withholding of tobacco from them is a terrible deprivation. The cost of supplying tobacco would not be excessive, and I think the advantage would be great.
When you come to the youthful offender, you are face to face with a mighty problem. Those who profess to speak with confidence on the subject of the criminal say that the youth of the criminal does not always indicate the enormity of the offence; that some of the wijrst men in the penitentiaries are those serving their first terms; that some of these are the most abandoned of the immates of the penitentiaries. I do not believe that you can make your line of segregation on the basis of age. If there is to be segregation, the less hardened of the criminals should be removed to an institution where they will not be subjected to the contaminating influences of what are called hardened criminals. I should like to see something done along the line of education. So many of these young boys that drift into the penitentiaries hardly know how to read or write; some cannot even sign their own names. It does seem almost a crime that young fellows sixteen, seventeen and eighteen years of age are incarcerated for three or four years during the constructive and acquiring period of their lives, and then turned out at the expiration of their term no better than they were when they went in. I agree with the member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) that the object of our penitentiary^systam should be punitive; but it should be reformative as well. I sincerely trust that when the opportunity arises the Minister of Justice will give his attention to the problems that I know he realizes must be solved, and will endeavour to do something to better the conditions of the criminal population of our country.

I repeat that I am not opposed to the granting of this bonus to the guards. I pointed out, however, that their pay, generally speaking, was better than the pay of many men in other 'branches of the service who had longer hours and greater responsibility. To that statement, which has a bearing upon the question of salary, or bonus to these men, the member for Kingston did not take any exception, although he came to the conclusion that I was opposed to the granting of an increase

to the guards of the institution. That, of course, will go on record, and I trust that it will bring to him the reward that he expects it will. Of course I am not responsible for what the hon. gentleman thought; Hansard will show what I said.
In the matter of gratuities, I should have thought that a gentleman so well posted in these matters as the member for Kingston would have been more familiar with the subject wilth which he was dealing. He said that this gratuity was given not to those who voluntarily resigned their positions, but only to those who resigned on account of illness, who had reached old age in the service, or whose condition of health compelled them to retire. My hon, friend is entirely in error in that, because gratuities have been' given in more than one case to guards who resigned not on account of ill-health. The Minister of Justice will bear me out in that assertion.
Of course, I did not profess to cover' every class. I understand that gratuities are at times granted when guards are permitted to resign to promote efficiency.
My hon. friend is now giving us a supplement to his former statement. Of course, I can only take his remarks as he gave them. My point is that his former statement is entirely incorrect
Partially.
No, entirely incorrect. He said that this gratuity was not given to guards who voluntarily resigned their positions.
I say that yet.

I am in a position to state that that is incorrect. During the present year guards who have resigned not because of ill health or decrepitude have applied for gratuity and' have received it.
I can give the names if necessary. I am more than pleased that the member for Kingston, who has given this matter a great deal of study, has agreed with one or two of the assertions that I made. It is a satisfaction and an encouragement to me that he agrees with me in the matter of supplying tobacco to the convicts. I was sorry that he did not see fit to express a definite opinion in regard to the employment of convicts in work for the State, in the making of furniture and other things in general use in various departments of the Government. There is nothing in the breaking of stone to improve the mental,
moral or physical condition of the convict. That has been going on as far back as I can remember; the practice still prevails in all these institutions. I do not agree that it would be wise to get agricultural employment for all the convicts, because many of them are unsuited to agricultural work. Many of them are mechanically inclined. There is a farm connected with each of these institutions which I think, will give employment to most of those among the convicts who are suited to that kind of work and who can be benefited by engaging in it. Hundreds of convicts could be employed in learning trades, making furniture, manufacturing things which the State must buy in large quantities, such as rural mail boxes, and the like. It is only necessary to visit one of these institutions and observe the difference between the convicts employed on the stone piles and those employed at making brooms or some other kind of work to realize the great benefit that is to be derived from utilizing the convicts in some constructive employment. Work on roads is very useful; it is work in the open; the convict has something to show for his labour and something to look forward to. Various penal institutions on the other side of the line recognize the benefit of engaging these men to work on the roads. I understand that the convicts are often taken many miles from the gates of the prison in order	that
they may be employed in this way. I mentioned that piece of road near Barrie-field camp because it is a government road. It is ,a road which has been taken over by the Dominion Government and which has to be maintained by the Dominion Government, and when prison labour could easily be employed it is reasonable that it should be employed in maintaining a piece of property owned by this Government.
To the other and main point to which I referred, the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Niokle) did not give his attention, that is, the building of an institution for the care of boys of 21 years of age who are first offenders, and I would like to have an expression of opinion on that point from the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Different matters have been touched upon, and perhaps I might say just a word or two with Tegard to them. I shall be very glad to express to the committee the opinion I hold with regard to providing means whereby certain institu-



tions cmight be created for different classes of offenders, and I shall deal with that after I 'have said a few words about other matters that have been mentioned. With regard to the question of gratuities and its bearing upon the particular case in which a compassionate allowance was granted, I would like to point out that in no department of the Civil Service is there provision made for compensation to surviving relatives of employees'. In some of the departments, with regard to older civil servants, who were in the employment of the Government when the superannuation! system was in force, there is provision for superannuation, but that does not survive the recipient of it. The penitentiaries, therefore, are not in a different position with regard to the granting of compensation to the surviving relatives of servants who have died in their employ from the other departments of IGovern-ment. The committee will realize that it would be a large proposition, which would call for careful consideration by this Government, to undertake to make provision for surviving relatives of its employees. Much might be said in favour of that plan, but I do not see that anything special might be said in favour of it so far as tbe employees of penitentiaries are concerned. The gratuity is intended as an allowance for a man who serves either for a lengthy period until he is broken down, or whose employment in the penitentiary is terminated otherwise than by fault of his own. There are cases in which men resign because they become incapacitated, and it is usual in such cases to grant a gratuity. There are also cases in which it is considered that it tends to promote the efficiency of the institution that a man should be retired or allowed to resign, and in such cases the gratuity is paid to him.
