But so far as there is any connection between the granting of the compassionate allowance, granted1 to Mrs. Mackenzie in the supplementary estimates, and the question of gratuities, I have only to point out that to make any grant to the surviving dependents, we have to depart from the rule that prevails throughout the Civil Service. The special circumstances to which I referred when I said that I thought there was reason to believe that there would not be many absolutely similar cases was not an expression of opinion as to the liability of other men dying from heart disease. Mr. Mackenzie had a record of service that was absolutely exceptional in its length, as I am informed by the officers of the peniten-
tiary, and there was in the second place this fact that played a large part in leading to the conclusion that the case should be treated as exceptional, that is to say, that his widow, with a large family of very small children', was left in absolutely destitute circumstances. 1 am also told that the case stood out rather as an exception, in that combination of conditions, with regard to what ordinarily happens in the case of a penitentiary vote. With regard to this particular allowance which is the matter properly before the committee, I have only to say that, in fixing the amount of it and the limit with regard to salaries to those who should be recipients of it, we have followed what has been done in the great number of departments of this Government, in view of the high cost of living. Some observations have been made with regard to the remuneration which those men already receive. That remuneration w.as fixed by Statute some years ago, Parliament ,at that time thinking it a proper remuneration fur the services. If Parliament was right in that regard, then there must exist for those employees the same reason resting upon the increased cost of living that applies in the case of the employees of the Government generally. As to the limitation of $1,000, that, as I s.ay, is following the rule. Tt has been pointed out that, ini the supplementary estimates with regard to the post office, provision has been made for this allowance with regard to men of ,a certain class of employment who receive .a salary up to $1,600. When we come to deal with that item, I think I shall be in a position to explain the reason of that particular disposition with regard to that particular department.
Something has been said with regard to the utilization of prison labour. I quite *sympathise with the idea that we should utilize our prison labour to turn out a product that might be used by the Government and that might afford for the men in the penitentiaries more suitable occupation than sometimes we are able to put them to. It should, however, be remembered that it does not depend upon the Department of Justice to furnish things to people who do not want to take them from it. Before we can find our way to furnish those things, we shall have to find our market with the other departments of Government. It does not belong to me to criticise nor do I intend to do so, but we cannot supply that for which there is no demand. I have at different times, since I have had charge of the

administration of the penitentiaries, sought to find an outlet for penitentiary labour in furnishing the requirements of other departments. I regret to say I have not been successful. I do not want to criticise the reasons that were given. They were, in the judgment of those .administering those departments, sufficient reasons, and I think at that particular time they were not open to criticism. .
In that connection, referring to what the hon. member for North Oxford has said with regard to pay, iif we were put in a position where the product of the labour of the convict could be disposed of to other departments of the Government, or in other directions that would not bring us into unfair competition with free labour, I myself would believe that it would be a perfectly proper thing that these things should be paid for by whomsoever they were acquired, and that out of those moneys there should be paid something to the convict to represent wages. In talking of wages or pay it has to be remembered that a convict is supported and clothed, but I think it would be most desirable, provided the moneys so paid to him for his labour were not necessary for the maintenance of those depending upon him while he was in the penitentiary-which is the first purpose .to which it should be devoted-that when he went out he should have some savings to his credit. I certainly would *welcome the day when it would be possible to bring about that condition of affairs. But it does not depend upon those responsible for the penitentiaries whether this is to be done or not. We cannot sell our product and get money for it until there are people ready to buy our product and pay for it. There have been certain periods, at the outbreak of this war for instance, when there was a serious lack of employment in the ordinary industries of the country, and apprehension of a greater lack of employment. At that time, at all events, it would hardly have seemed desirable to press for the initiation of a system of utilization of penitentiary labour. But we have done something towards the utilization of that labour in connection with the farming industry, and although I am not in a position to give details at the present moment, I may say that we have also utilized prison labour to a certain extent in the direction of providing things necessary in connection with the interned alien prisoners. I shall be glad, if it should become possible for us to find an outlet for the product of our labour, not only to give consideration to,
but if the matter be in my hands, to endeavour to bring into practical operation, a system whereby more useful work may be done and whereby we may obtain the very desirable thing suggested by the hon. member for North Oxford. With regard to the separation of prisoners, I quite agree that it would be highly desirable to have a separation of the prisoners' according to classes. I am not absolutely clear that it would have to be according to age, though I dare say you would find a larger proportion amongst the younger criminals who ought to be classified as among the less hardened criminals, than you would perhaps find among older men. I would rather classify with regard to the character of the criminal you are dealing with than absolutely on the line of age. I may say that before the outbreak of this war, in the year of 1914, I had given very considerable thought to this matter, and the plan that I had conceived, though not absolutely the plan suggested by the hon. member for Frontenac, was somewhat along the same line. My impression was, and still is, that the hardened criminal is in the minority, and my conception of what would be desirable to do, and what I should be glad to do if it should become possible and I have the opportunity, would be to provide say, two institutions in which the more hardened class of criminals should be confined, leaving the present institutions for what I believe to be the majority of the criminals we handle, that is, those who would not be described as hardened criminals. I think there would be advantage in preserving thajse Hess, hardened from the injurious influence of association with those who are more hardened. In the second place, there would be to my mind this great advantage, that if you divide the institutions in that way it -would make it possible to adopt what might be described as a milder rule for the institutions generally, reserving the more severe features of the rules as they are deemed necessary, for those institutions where the hardened criminals would be confined. Plans of that kind, of course, involve the starting out in new enterprise in the way of public works, and the expenditure of public money, and it was not considered desirable that we should embark upon new enterprises of that kind at that time to which I have referred. I do hope, however, that under better and more favourable circumstances we shall be able to obtain the result of a separation on the lines 1 have indicated, and I do hope that when we come to more normal times and condi-

tions it may be possible to persuade those who might properly be the customers of the penitentiary of the advisability of giving their custom to the penitentiary. When that time comes I shall certainly be glad to do what depends upon me, if I should be responsible for the administration of the institutions, to avail ourselves of that opportunity of giving a more varied employment.
Something has been said about road-making as a desirable form of employment. 1 think the hon. member will admit that we have done some little road-making during the past summer. As to the advantage ot disadvantage, I may say that those who are experienced in the administration of pen-itentaries-I am not now expressing my own opinion-do not look uipon it as desirable that the men should be called .away to work at distances from the institution. While they sympathize with the desire for giving more suitable work, these experienced people do not seem to be of the opinion that road-making, outside of the immediate surroundings of the penitentiary would be a desirable thing.
Both hon. gentlemen have said something about tobacco, and I must admit that they touch what ought to he a very responsive chord in my own heart. The matter has been discussed from time to time with those responsible for 'the administration of the penitentiaries. What is said with regard to it -and I must say it has not quite convinced me that we ought not to allow tobacco- is that if you permit the use of tobacco for smoking purposes, that, of course involves tlie possession of matches and the possible danger of fire, which is an institution of that kind, no matter what you do to make it fireproof, is not ito be overlooked. Such a thing in such an institution would be a disaster. Then, of course, it leaves open the practices of allowing tobacco to be chewed. Now it has been urged upon me that if we allow the use of tobacco it will be availed of, of course, by those who had contracted the habit before they went into the penitentiary, and in all probability by those who had not acquired the habit when they entered the penitentiary. It has been pressed upon me-I do not say it is a conclusive argument- that it would 'be a very undesirable thing if, among other habits, a young convict might acquire in a stay of two or three years in a penitentiary, would be the habit of chewing tobacco.
I do not want to say that personally I am specially scandalized by the suggestion, but there are people whose opinions are

certainly entitled to very great respect, who would look upon that as a most objectionable thing. However, with regard to the question of tobacco, as I say, I am not convinced that it would not be desirable to permit its use, and I am not saying my last word upon the subject, if we can find a means which will satisfy those responsible for the administration that we are not creating inconveniences which would more than counterbalance the privation to which the men are now subject, and the more serious evil which is occasioned 'by the prohibition of tobacco, that is the trafficking between guards and prisoners.
How is the tobacco which is thus trafficked in used? Is it smoked or chewed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have cases where men have been punished for smoking. We also have cases where men are found using tobacco for chewing purposes. Without pretending to speak with absolute certainty, my impression would be that it is used more for chewing than for smoking. One obvious reason is that the violation of the rule is lass perfectly manifest if the tobacco is used for chewing. The convict has a better opportunity to avoid detection in the use of tobacco for chewing purposes.

If I understood 'the hon. member for Frontenae correctly, he is under the impression that this gratuity is an optional gratuity, that is, it is paid provided the authorities see fit, and withheld if the -authorities do not see fit to pay it. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It may be withheld if the man's course of conduct is considered to lbe such as would not entitle him to it. I may say, however, that, generally speaking, unless a man's connection with the penitentiary terminates either of his*own perfect volition, when he is able to remain on, and when there is no reason to part with him, unless he has been guilty of conduct which is really reprehensible, it is usual to grant the gratuity. The man, however, may forfeit it by bad conduct.
I am speaking of the $100.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is an allowance to all the employees who have salaries of $1,000 and less. It is not optional.
It is simply a temporary increase of salary without any option.
Yes.

I understand the argument of my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) to be that being optional it placed the officer more dependent upon the favour of his superior than upon good service, whereas if he gets it as a straight increase in salary, of course he is still independent.

Perhaps I did not make myself clear. I was not referring to this $100 at all. I was referring to the gratuity which is given to a man when he retires after serving, say, ten, or fifteen, or twenty years.

further amount required, $1,800 ; to provide an amount for the Deputy Speaker of the House of Commons in lieu of apartments, for the year ending 31st March, 1918, at the rate of $5 per diem-further amount required, $600 ; annuity to Dr. Thomas Barnard Flint, upon his retirement from the Clerkship of the House of Commons through physical disability, $2,500- $59,900.

This item of $55,000 is put in to cover the extra fifteen day's allowance to members. It also provides an amount of $2,500 to Dr. Beland and makes provision for lose on account of death. This is to take the place of the item we had in the previous estimates.
The other items will not be used?

It will not be used. The
amounts of $1,800 and $600 are necessary to cover the allowance to the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker on account of the session being so much longer than was expected. Then we have an item of $2,500 for an annuity to Dr. Flint upon his retirement from the clerkship of the House of Commons. I may say in reference to this item that we all know that Dr. Flint's health has not been very good and that he wishes to retire. I have been in the House all the time that Dr. Flint has occupied the position he now has; in fact I was here while Dr. Flint was ,a member of the House. We all feel sorry that his health is such that it is necessary for him to retire. He has been a splendid official, liked by every member of the House and it is a matter of regret to us that we are about to lose him. Still, these things must come and it is at his own request that he retires. The amount of $2,500 allowed as an annuity, Dr. Flint himself feels is fair and reasonable and he is quite satisfied with it. Therefore, I hope the House will allow this item to go through.

I have not been in the House nearly so long as my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) but I have been here for ten years -and I have had occasion to form a critical judgment of the devotion which Dr. Flint has shown, to his duties. He has given entire satisfaction, I think, to all the members of the House. One thing which I think it is proper to re* fer to is the fact that he has displayed very great industry in editing the work of Dr. Bourinot. He has added many most valuable notes and citations which are of very great assistance to members. His book will certainly remain as a monument to his very great industry and ability. I feel sure that my hon. friend expresses the

feelings of all the members of this House when he says that it is with the deepest regret that we learn of the -infirmity which makes it necessary for Dr. Flint to retire. I am also convinced that the recognition which the 'Government has asked the House to give him in -the way of a retiring /allowance will be very cheerfully approved of by the House.

I desire to add to the
observations made by my -hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) and my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) by expressing my regret that Dr Flint finds it necessary, owing to the unsatisfactory condition of his health, to retire from the very honourable and respected position of Clerk of this House. He has served many years in a public capacity and he has attained to the highest official position that could be occupied by any man in this House. It so happened when Dr Flint retired from the office of Clerk Assistant of the Legislative Assembly of Nova Scotia in 1891 I succeeded him. Since that time the relations existing between Dr Flint and myself have been of the most cordial and agreeable character. I could not say anything that would add to the esteem that Dr Flint has won for himself among the members of this House in both political parties. I speak of him both as a member of the House of Commons and an official of the House for several years. Before he assumed the position of clerk, he was representative of the county of Yarmouth in Nova Scotia for several years, and as the representative of that county he won the respect and good feeling of all his associates in the House of Commons. I can only express the wish that Dr Flint may be long spared -and that the condition of his health will permit him to continue to render useful service if not to the Dominion of Canada, to the province of Nova Scotia, for many years to come.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think it would be hardly fitting that this item should go through without my saying a word along the line of the observations of those who have preceded me. It has been my privilege and pleasure to be more or less intimately associated with Dr Flint more particularly during the past two years. I can bear tribute to his unfailing courtesy and consideration to me, sometimes under somewhat trying circumstances. I know that only one desire animated Dr Flint in his public service, whether as a member or as Clerk of this House, and that was to serve to the very best of his ability. No one regrets more than the clerk himself the

infirmity which makes it absolutely necessary that this vote should appear in the estimates. I only hope that the House may be fortunate enough to have a successor in the office who will carry out the traditions as creditably as Dr Flint has.

In this item, No. 512,
there are four amounts the first of which is $55,000. I understood the minister to say that it was in substitution
11 p.m. for .the item, of $22,010 which appeared in the first supplementary estimates, page 5. If that .be the case, it strikes me the phraseology of the preceding grant of $55,000 is not apt.

This item is changed. Item 416 reads:
To provide payment of the full sesional indemnity of members of the House of Commons 

days lost through absence caused by illness, public business, being engaged in necessary farming operations, or on account of death, during the present session, including an amount of $2,500 to Hon. H. S. BSland, a prisoner of war in Germany, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in chapter 10 of the Revised Statutes, an Act respecting the Senate and House of Commons or any amendments thereto-payment to be made as the Treasury Board may direct, $22,010.
This item is changed for this reason. The session has been about twice as long as the ordinary session, and it was arranged that fifteen days over and above the fifteen days that are allowed under the statute should be allowed to the members for absence, and the item had to be remodelled to cover that arrangement. I thought the item covered the senators' absence also, but I do not know whether it can be interpreted in that way. However, as we have it now I think it is quite satisfactory to all parties.
Is it in substitution for the other item, or in addition?
It is in substitution. The other item would not allow the extra fifteen days, so that we just substitute this item for the other.
I understand that item 416, just referred) to by the hon. minister and the hon. member for Russell, is not to be concurred in, or not to be used in any event.

It is- all in item 416. We will concur in that, but it will not be used. This item now takes the place of 416. There are a great many items in 416, and we are just putting in this item to take the place of item 416.
Should not the other be stricken out?	.
We can strike it out, but it is not necessary. I thought it would not make much difference.
It is not good practice to vote two amounts for the one purpose. When the Speaker is in the Chair, by unanimous consent it can be stricken out.
I have not gone into it, but t-herS is nothing in that item, as far as 1 can see, that is different from the other, but if the House will let it go through as it is, the money will not be used.

There is an additional
amount provided by this item, because this amount is larger than the other item.
As I understood the Finance Minister, it took the place of the other, and they have added a sufficient amount to cover the absences. Possibly there may be some difference.
If the other item is included in this, then it would be very easy, by unanimous consent of the House, to strike it out.
I am going to propose concurrence after we put these items through, and if there is any objection, I will strike it out.

Another point in connection with this vote is that it appears to me that the Government, by the phraseology of the vote, is placing a premium upon absence -in this House, encouraging the members who stay away, and punishing those who remain. According to this vote as it stands at the present time, the member who has been away thirty days or more will receive a bonus, or a re-vote of $225.

The hon. gentleman states that the Government is paying a premium on absence. This matter was arranged by the whips on both sides of the House. If there is any misunderstanding, I am not assuming any responsibility in the matter. I understand both whips agreed that, on account of the length of the session, the extra fifteen days should be allowed. If I am wrong, I should like the whips to say so.

I am perfectly willing to withdraw the remark that the Government was placing a premium on absence because I do not think it was done intentionally. I do not dispute the fact that the whips may have come to such an agreement, but I think every member of this House has the right to give his own opinion concern-

ing the votes brought before the House, and I am sure the few words which I am going to utter will meet with the approval, I will not say of the majority of members but of a large number. The item, as it stands at present, amounts to this: that a member who has been absent for thirty days or more during this session is receiving $225 more than he would receive if this vote had not been put through. A member who has been absent say 18 days is receiving $45 more than he would receive if this vote were not put through, but the member who has attended to his parliamentary duties from the beginning of the session is receiving absolutely not one cent more than he would receive if the vote had not been put through. In this way those who. were absent 30 days or more are receiving a reward for their absence. Those who have been absent less than 30 days, but more than 15 days, are receiving a reward, but a less reward than the man who has been, away longer. Those who have remained here during the entire [DOT]session, or wlm have lost less than 15 days, receive no reward at all. I spoke about it to the Speaker a few moments ago, and he explained to me that it would, of course, be impossible to change this vote at the present time without a new authorization from the Governor General and a new estimate, hut I thought it only right to bring this point to the attention of the House. The member who has been away -from this House attending to his private business, who has not -been obliged to pay his living expenses in Ottawa for the time he was away, and who was undoubtedly making money in his own private affairs while absent from the House, is receiving a reward of $225. It appears to me to be illogical, and I think it would be a great deal fairer if the Government would consider the matter before the close of the session and introduce an item to add to the sessional indemnity of the other members the sum of $225, which you are giving to the members who- were absent 30 days. In that way those who have been absent more than 30 days would, be getting absolutely what they are getting under this vote, and the member who has, been present during the entire session or absent less than 15 days, would be rewarded accordingly for his attendance here. Every one knows the session has been a lengthy one. That a large number of members have been unavoidably absent, I am willing to admit. On the other .hand, there are others who certainly would have absented themselves to 
attend to their private business if they had known this vote was to be put through at the last moment.
I do not think that an hon. member should be punished for remaining in this House. Western members, .for instance, who have been here the whole session, should not b.; punished for having remained in attendance. I admit that I have missed more than the fifteen days; therefore, the vote does not affect me as much as it affects members who have remained in the Honse. But as a matter of justice to every one, the Government should give this .matter serious consideration. It should be possible tomorrow to bring in an estimate or to change the phraseology of this item with a view to providing that all members shall be treated alike. It has been pointed out that if this were done the amount of the vote would necessarily be increased. Well, there are 180 members in this House, and to give the allowance of $225 to each member would mean a vote of only $40,500. The amount of the vote ais it appears in the estimates now is $55,000; moreover, those who have been absent more than 15 days would not receive as much as $225, and a certain amount would not be used. I think that that is a fair proposal, and would do justice to all members. If I used the expression that the Government was placing a premium upon absence, I did not mean to s.ay that they were doing so intentionally. That was, perhaps, an impolite expression of what I had in my mind-that the absent member was being rewarded while the man who remained here was being punished for hie attendance.

I hope that nobody will go away with the impression that under the proposed resolution any member of the House is going to get more than his sessional indemnity, $2,500. As this session has been practically double the length of an ordinary session, it was thought that the exemption should be for double the usual period. Under the law as it stands at present some men are absent only two days, five days, during the session, while others take their full fifteen days and get their full indemnity. In this ease we have applied exactly the same principle, so far as I can see, as that which has hitherto prevailed. On the basis that there should be fifteen days' exemption for a four months' session, we are providing for an exemption of thirty days for an eight months' session. This is the only method we could adopt without passing a special

Act increasing the indemnity, and I am sure that none of the members are in favour of doing that.
Would it not be advisable to add to the end of this item the words "payment to be made as the Treasury Board may direct"? These words are usually placed at the end of such items as this.

I think that that can he done.
I move that after "1906" at the end of item 512 the words "payment to be made as the Treasury Board may direct" be inserted.
Amendment agreed to.

I wish to say a word in connection with this allowance for days of absence. I do not propose to make any motion on the subject, but it is only fair that there should be an understanding as to the different positions of members of the House coming from different sections of the country. Those of us who come from a considerable distance-from west of Lake Superior, from the Maritime Provinces, and from some constituencies in the more remote portions of Ontario and Quebec-are unable to carry on our private business while attending to the public business of the session. It appears that the members who are situated within a night's or an afternoon's railroad run of the city of Ottawa are in a position to carry on their private business while ostensibly attending to their duties in Parliament. Those of us who are not so fortunately situated have nJo right to find fault with tiho-se who-are, provided the exercise "of their liberties does not reflect upon us and do us substantial injury. As a matter of fact, the business of this House is and has been delayed session after session by the fact that such a large proportion of members live within a comparatively short distance of the capital and make it a matter of business to be absent from the House the latter end of the week and the beginning cf the week thereafter. So that during the greater part of the session, instead of doing business five days in the week, we are doing business three days in the week, and sometimes hardly that. That has the effect of lengthening the session unduly; it compels the men who reside at a distance to remain 'here weeks and months longer than they would be required to remain if everybody stayed here and attended to business during the five or six days of the week. The penalty of a fine of $15 for each day's absence was imposed for the purpose of holding members to their work. We relieved them of that fine to the extent
of fifteen days-and it is this fifteen days that has done the damage so far. Now we propose to make that fifteen days thirty days. On the one hand we declare that the interests of the country and the treasury shall be protected by a fine of $15 against each member who is absent from a day's sitting, and then we provide that the fine shall not be paid in respect of fifteen days. Now we provide that the fine -shall not he paid in respect of thirty days. The position is entirely illogical. While it would, perhaps, be ineffective to make any determined opposition to this- vote, I take the responsibility, following the remarks of the member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin), of placing before the House the serious disadvantage to which a large proportion of the members are subjected by reason of the undue exercise on the part of other members of the privilege and advantage of attending to their private business while the session is in progress.

My hon. friend stated a moment ago that according to the law it was impossible to increase the sessional indemnity. What would prevent the Government from calling it a certain amount for expenses on account of the session being iSO m-uch longer than usual? The word " expenses " is used in -this item, and the same amount could he given to every hon. member to allow for expenses which have increased on account of the length of the session. It is well known that the cost of living in Canada has increased tremendously, and Ottawa is no exception. I think my suggestion would cover the objection of my hon. friend who stated a moment ago that, according to -the law of the land, we could not increase the indemnity. It would not be increasing the indemnity if we called it an 'appropriation for extraordinary expenses on account of the length of the session. M-any of us are obliged to remain here during the whole sess'sion, and I do -not w-an-t to be penalized -I do not use the word offensively-because we are just as much entitled to that a-moumt of money -as are others who have been away.

The hon. -member, from his parliamentary experience, of course, knows that it is impossible to change this item -as- it is now in the estimates. As this is a money -Bill, the assent of His Excellency the Governor General must be Obtained, and the appropriation is inserted this session in -almost exactly the same way as it has been inserted in other years, with the

exception that fifteen days extra have heen allowed. I understood froim the Chief Whips of both sides that hon. members thought that this was a fair and reasonable thing to do. There are many members who have been here practically the whole session who have lost thirty days. *1 know one member in this House who, in order to attend his business, leaves on Friday afternoon for his home-and he has to go a long distance-and gets back here on Tuesday. Yet he is here Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday until probably 4 p.m. On a session like this he would lose fifteen days, and yet he has done as much work as many others who have been here, because probably he may have taken an active part. There are, therefore, cases in which it would be hardly fair not to make a	little	extra	allowance on
account of the session lasting eight months.	There is no way in which
I can change this vote, and as it was understood to be agreeable to members on both sides, the Government asked His Excellency for permission to insert this item just as has been done in other years on account of days lost through absence caused by illness, public business, or on account of death, with the exception that fifteen extra days have been added.
I do not understand that the hon. gentlemen who have spoken have objected to the additional allowance of fifteen days.
They wanted .a change.

The suggestion is that, in order, to do complete justice, some further provision should be made. There is a strange anomaly in this vote, in that it provides that a member of the House of Commons should be allowed only an extra fifteen days on account of absence through illness and so on, but in respect to our good friends in the Senate, they may be allowed a full sessional indemnity if they happen to be ill in a hospital more than ten miles from Ottawa. The result of that is that a senator who happens to be ill at his home and goes to a hospital for attendance receives his full sessional' indemnity provided that his illness lasts during the whole session, while a member of the House of Commons, being equally ill and requiring medical treatment in a hospital, is allowed only an extra fifteen days' indemnity. I think the vote should be changed to make it applicable equally to members of the Senate and members of the House of Com-

mons. It occurs to me that a fair additional vote to bring down, in, order to do even a small measure of justice to members from the West who come here from a long distance, would be to .make .a special provision which would be particularly applicable to this session. As the minister knows, there is an allowance for expenses in coming to the opening of Parliament and in returning home after prorogation. During the present session Parliament adjourned in February and re-assembled in April, but the expenses of going home and returning, which were equally as great as those in coming to the opening of Parliament and in returning after prorogation, are not allowed for, and the members are obliged to pay their own expenses both in coming and going. It would be a small measure of justice to members who come from a long distance to give them those expenses. It would not affect me very much because my expenses in coming here are comparatively sma?and I am, therefore, free to speak about the [DOT] matter. I am also thankful to say that I am not affected by the fifteen days' provision-, because I have not lost fifteen days during this session. While the item as to the fifteen days is right, it ought to be made uniform with regard to the Senate and the House of Commons. The minister may have put it in in this way in order to please the Senate. He is elever at framing legislation to pass both Houses.

I cannot change the item as
iifc appears in. (the estimates, .and I think we shall have to let it go through.
There is plenty of time. Parliament does not .prorogue to-night. If the minister wants to do a thing in a hurry, he can do it.

There is not any opportunity for aniy further (estimate 'being brought down. I would like to have these put through and concurred in, I understand the only matter that is left and that might delay prorogation is the War-time Elections Act, which has to come back from the Senate.
That cannot get through for two days yet.
It has passed the Senate and will be here to-morrow.
It has to be put on the Order Paper, and it could not be taken up to-morrow.

I am sure the minister will find that there will be a desire on the part of hon. members to discuss fully any amendments that may havie been made to that Bill. If, therefore, the minister approves my suggestion, there will be ample time toi bring down a supplementary estimate.

I am. willing to bring my
hon. friend's suggestion to the attention of the Government, hut we would like to have that Bill proceeded with to-morrow, and then we could take the necessary time to discuss it. We do not want it to be pressed through the House faster than is necessary. I think every one of us is anxious to get away, and we should all be ready to facilitate matters as much as possible. I should like to get this item through.

This would be a very little matter to dispose of to-morrow, if the suggestion meets with my hon. friend's approval. If we are only waiting for the Franchise Bill, in the ordinary course if it does not come down until to-morrow it will not get on the Order Paper until Saturday, and we shall be kicking our heels around here all day to-morrow. Perhaps we could not be better employed than in doing justice to our western friends.
Lighthouse and coast service *- Further amount required to pay pensions to retired pilots, viz.: O. Noel, F. X. Desmeules, and Adjutor Baillargeon, $800.

This relates to the
ughthouse and coast service. I want to call the attention of the minister to the ,act that early in the session a question was put to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, as to whether it was proposed to' give Lhe lighthouse keepers an increase in salary. There have been a great many increases given by Parliament upon the invitation of the Government during this session, most of which were pretty strenuously opposed on this side of the House. In answer to that question, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries said that he could not hold out any hope of an increase. It is within my knowledge that there are a great many lighthouse keepers who are getting a salary, some of them, of only $300 a year. The average salary is from $300 to $400, I am informed. These men are leading a lonely life in a lighthouse upon a
rock, and in the winter especially their life is surrounded with great hardships; and to expect men to continue to perform those arduous duties and undergo the hardships they are compelled to undergo for the small salary of $300 is to my mind not at all creditable to a country like Canada. I regret very much that the minister was not able to give some assurance that the representations which have been made to him would be favourably entertained, and I would ask the minister now whether ho could see his way clear to bringing down before the close of this session .an item,	providing	for	an
increase of even $100 a year for these men. They are affected by the high cost of living just as other people are, and the salaries which they receive may truly be called starvation salaries. They cannot live upon them. In some cases lighthouse keepers can make some money out of fishing, but those cases are the exceptions. The great majority have nothing but their salaries, which are entirely inadequate for them to live upon and to bring up their families.

I will bring the matter before the members of Council to-morrow and see whether anything can be done.
To complete special allowance to the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada to cover travelling and other expenses in connection with his services while acting as Deputy to His Excellency the Governor General, $2,500.
I should like a little explanation of this item. I am informed that the salary of the Chief Justice of Canada is $10,000 a year. Is that correct?
Yes.
I am also informed that he receives an allowance of $2,500 for travelling expenses when he goes overseas to attend the meetings of the Privy Council. Is that right?
Yes, he is a member of the Privy Council.

I presume he has not attended many sittings during the last three years. As I understand it, he now receives $2,500 for signing his name for the Governor-General. We propose here to add another $2,500, making $5,000 which the Chief Justice will receive to cover travelling and other expenses in connection with his services while acting as deputy to His Excellency the Governor-General. I am informed that the Chief Justice lives in Ottawa. Is that right?
Yes.

If he is within the city limits, his travelling expenses ought not to be very heavy. I do not believe this increase of $2,500 is warranted. I do not believe there is a man in this House who believes it is warranted, and I am going to test the feeling of the committee by moving that the item be struck out.

The hon. member is correct in stating that the salary of the Chief Justice is $10,000. The Chief Justice has also been receiving $5,000 per annum to cover travelling and other expenses in connection with his services while acting as Deputy to His Excellency the Governor General. It is true the Chief Justice lives in Ottawa, but there are times when he may be a considerable distance away and has to return to the city. We had $5,000 in itihe estimates last year for this purpose, but through some error, the .amount was put in at $2,500 this year, and we are simply asking that the item be restored to the usual amount. It is not an increase at all. The other item of $2,500 in the main estimates is to cover the expenses of the Chief Justice when attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. I hardly think it would be fair to reduce the item by $2,500. I am sorry this mistake w.as made in preparing the estimates, and I would ask the House to agree to the $2,500 being restored.

I do not want to be unreasonable, but $5,000 for signing one's name a few times does .seem to nre to be piling it on pretty thick. Ten thousand dollars as Chief Justice, and five thousand dollars as Deputy to the Governor General makes fifteen thousand a year. I do not think the time and work of the Chief Justice can begin to be compared with the time and work of the Prime Minister and the leader of the Opposition.
It seems to me to be entirely unreasonable that a gentleman living right here in Ottawa should receive. $5,000 for occasionally signing his name. If we want to increase the salary of the Chief Justice of Canada, let us put it in as increase in salary. Personally, I think this item might very well be cut out altogether. I think the Chief Justice of Canada or some other "justice living here in Ottawa could, without receiving any pay for it, sign his name a few times, if the Governor General happens to he away on his holidays. In regard to those trips, overseas, I do not know whether I am right or not, but I have heard it stated that the Chief Justice has drawn the $2,500

for travelling and other expenses in connection with attending the Privy Council in England, when, as a matter of fact, he never left Canada, but still drew the amount, taking it as part of his salary. Hon. gentlemen spoke here a while ago to the effect that the minister might bring in a little item which would hand- a couple of hundred dollars to various, members of this House who had been regular in their attendance, in order to even things up, that is, that a 'small amount might be granted; the western members and those from the extreme East, in consideration of the extra expense they were put to on account of the break in the session. This is something which would have to receive very earnest, and careful, and prayerful consideration, before it could be put through, but a matter of $5,000 to the Chief Justice of Canada for simply scribbling hi6 name a few times is dead easy.	.

The salary of the Chief Justice is $10,000. Merely expressing my own personal opinion, and not referring to the present Chief Justice or any one else in particular, I would say the naan who is fit to occupy the position of Chief Justice of Canada is a man who could earn perhaps twice as much as $10,000. So far as the salary of the Prime Minister is concerned, there is no doubt in nay mind that the Prime Minister could earn three times as much as he does were he to relinquish the position he occupies, and go back to the practice of his profession. I say the same of the leader of the Opposition were he a young man. I do not think the Prime Minister or the leader of the Opposition is paid the amount to which they are severally entitled.

I will not discuss that. It has always been the custom to pay this amount to. the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, and the 'Government feel that as he has been receiving $5,000 for the position, it is hardly fair to reduce it. While I have no objection to the hon. member from Frontenae (Mr. Edwards) expressing his opinion, I would like the House to concur in this item.

The item is put in to cover " travelling and other expenses." I quite agree with my hon. friend from Fron-tenae (Mr. Edwards) that $5,000 seems a large item for " travelling and other ex-

penses." I think it would he ibetter to make an allowance to the Chief Justice as deputy Governor General, toy reason of the very high ,and honourable position he holds and by reason of the fact that he does discharge the duties of deputy Governor General. I think it would be better to put it on that distinct ground. To my mind it would not be proper to strike out the item, because the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada has always acted as deputy Governor General, and has always received an allowance. I do not knorw whether it was $5,000 per year. It certainly would seem rather ungracious to discriminate against the present occupant of that high position and refuse to treat him in the same way as his predecessors have been treated. I agree with the minister, that the salary of the Chief Justice of Canada is not by any means a large one. I think we pay the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners $15,000 a year, $5,000 a year more than the salary of the Chief Justice of Canada. The other day a vote was passed to pay the Chairman of the Bureau of Research $10,000 per annum. As has been stated, a lawyer in good practice in Canada can earn twice or three times as much as the salary of (the Chief Justice, and a gentleman oif the eminence of the Chief Justice could easily earn at the Bar from $25,000 to $50,000 per annum in the larger cities. I do not object to voting the amount. What I object to is the language of the vote and the way it is put, as " travelling and other expenses."
Post Office-Outside Service.
To increase the minimum salary of railway mail clerks from $500 to $600, and to raise the annual statutory increases of railway mail clerks from $50 to $100 in cases where the salary is over $800, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act or the Post Office Act; also to provide for the payment of provisional allowance of $100 each to Civil Service employees of the Outside Service of the Post Office Department whose salaries are $1,600 and under, and also to provide for the establishment of inspectorate at North Rattleford,_ Sask., $608,000.

I would like to direct
the attention of the Government to the Question of staff and non-staff post offices. For some reason best known to the Post Office Department, the man who is in a staff post office is a member of the Civil Service, is entitled to a pension, and his salary is increased from year to year under the Civil Service Act, whereas a man in another place, which may he just as large as some of the staff post offices but which is a non-staff post office, is not entitled to be a member of the Civil Service, is not
entitled to any pension, and his salary is not automatically increased under the Civil Service Act. Formerly, in those non-staff post offices, the postmaster got a percentage of the revenue, and he paid the clerks out of that percentage.
Later, that percentage was taken away from the postmaster, he was put on a fixed salary, and the clerks were also put upon fixed salaries. If the Acting Postmaster General will look into the matter he will find that clerks have been sixteen or eighteen years in the service and that they have never had one dollar of an increase during that period whilst the revenue of these offices has gone up tremendously. That is simply unjust. Why the hard and fast rule should be made by the department that one should be a staff office and that the other should not be a staff office, and that because there is this difference the employees in one office should have the right to belong to the Civil Service, to be entitled to pensions and to increases of salary, whereas the others are deprived of every one of these benefits, is something that 1 cannot understand. This is the most unjustifiable treatment that could be accorded to any class of men who are working for the State. In my own town there is a man who has been in the post office for eleven years. He has not received a dollar of increase in that time, and his hours are from seven in the morning until half-past eight at night. Other clerks are in the same position. There are men who have been employed for varying terms, some for as long as twenty years, and not a dollar of increase has been given. While I absolutely approve of the increase in the salaries of mail clerks, a recognition which they are very much entitled to, I do not see why the Government cannot take into consideration those men who belong to those non-staff post offices and who are receiving the same salaries as they have received for years while it costs fifty per cent more to live. Taking into consideration their terms of service, an increase in their salaries would be a simple act of justice on the part of the department, and that increase ought to be proportionately the same increase as is granted to the mail clerks by this vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have a very considerable sympathy with what the hon. member has just said. I am transiently and quite newly in charge of this department. I had my attention called to the system of semistaff post offices, and I have been somewhat puzzled as to what was the advantage

in maintaining that separate and distinct system. I understand the distinction is that in the first place you have a post office where the postmaster has a percentage of the revenue and he provides his own help. These offices are in certain cases converted into what are called semi staff offices, the Government taking the entire revenue and paying the salaries of the postmaster and clerks out of the revenue. I have had it in my mind to look into the whole reason for the existence of the system. But apart from that, this class of clebks is not dealt with in the present vote, because, if an 12 m. addition were to be paid to them it would he paid out of the revenue of the post office. I cannot say more than that I purpose to look into it to ascertain the reason for the differentiation, and if there be an apparent injustice I will endeavour to remedy it.

The provision of the item is to raise the annual statutory increase from $50 to $100 in cases where the salary is over $800. It would seem to me that the increase is more needed where the salary is 'below $800. There may be a reason for this, and if so, I would like my hon. friend to inform the committee regarding it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the item the minimum salary is being raised from $500 to $600. In. the past the lower salaries have been increased at the rate of $50 per annum and not at the rate of $100. A line was drawn 'between those who increased by $50 and those who increased by $100, and that, I understand, has been at $1,000. It is proposed to extend the increase of $100 to those having a salary of $800. There is a very limited class below that which is not dealt with.
Why not give it to the lower class?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The prayer of the petition that was put before me was to extend it so that clerks receiving salaries of over $800 should get the benefit. I am not clear -why there should be a distinction between those above and those below, but the grievance that was complained of was that while those getting over $1,000 got this annual in->. crease of $100 those below $1,000 did not. Therefore, those below $1,000 and above $800 had a grievance. That is why the distinction was .made. Frankly, I am not in a position to state why it was not extended to those receiving less than $800.

I see, also, that the vote is:
To provide for the payment of provisional allowance of $100 each to Civil Service employees of the Outside Service of the Post Office Department, whose salaries are $1,600 and under.
What is the effect of the words "provisional allowance?" Does that differentiate it from an annual increase? Is that a flat amount, given generally?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is a flat amount of $100. In the supplementary estimates there was an item to provide an allowance of $100 to employees of the Civil Service receiving under $1,000. That increase has been given, I think, in practically all the departments this year, to put the lower salaried men in a better position to meet the increased demands upon them by reason of the high cost of living. It has been done by way of an allowance without an increase of salary. This also is an allowance, hut the difference here is that in regard to post office clerks and certain classes of railway mail clerks it has been extended to those getting up to $1,600. While we are doing this under the guise of a temporary allowance the classes of clerks that are covered have in reality a very substantial ground of complaint of inequality between their position, from the point of view of salary, and that of Civil Service employees of a similar grade generally. I will give one instance. In 1914 legislation was passed by this House providing that the increase to the railway mail clerks should be at the rate of $100 per annum instead of $50 per annum, as it previously had been.
Both this House and the Senate concurred in the view that that was a proper provision, but, unfortunately for the railway mail clerks, they were not dealt with by the Bill applicable to the employees of the post offices generally, which was enacted at the same time, or shortly before. A provision for making their increase $100 a year, instead of $50, was contained in the Bill, which also contained certain provisions with regard to the charges, made to the newspapers for carrying the mail. The Senate, while it approved of what was done for the class of mail clerks, refused to assent to the provision with regard to the carriage of the newspapers. The Bill came back to this House, and the Postmaster General at the time refused to accept the amendment of the Senate in regard to the newspapers, and it was not found possible to bring the two Houses to an agreement upon that subject, and by reason of that disagreement,

for the last three years this class of clerks nave been getting an increase of $50 a year, whereas the other employees drawing similax salaries were receiving an increase of $100 a year. These clerks pressed -unfortunately at a late period of the session-for a re-enactment of the legislation of 1914, and further pressed that it should be made, as seems to me only fair, to count from the time it was origin-ally passed, so that they might be on a footing of equality with their fellow employees. When this matter was brought to my attention, and the attention of the Government generally, it was too late to deal with It by legislation during the present session, and after an interview with the gentlemen, in which they put their case strongly, they acquiesced in the view that it was too late to do anything, and expressed their readiness to accept, as compensation, at all events for the past, this allowance of $100 for this year. We look forward in the future to rectify the injustice done to then. For the time being we are giving something less than they would have received if that legislation had been passed at the time, by way of compensation, for what I really think they have been unfairly deprived of by the accident which happened in regard to the Bill.
This refers to Civil Service employees of the Outside Service. What does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand it would cover every class of employee in the Post Office Department of the Outside Service. We are not making a distinction between the different classes. We have letter carriers and clerks and they are subdivided mto different classes. There are railway mail clerks, clerks in the Service, in the post office, letter carriers, and a large number of different denominations of employees, and we use the word "employees" to make it cover everybody.
Mr. McKENZIE .[DOT] I desire to bring to the notice of the House a question which I think deserves consideration. We have a certain body of officials around this building called messengers. I do not know that their employment comes under any department. Perhaps the Speaker's jurisdiction, covers this class more than any other juris-tion. I was asked by some of those very useful gentlemen who are employed around the building to bring their case to the notice of the Government, and I would just as soon bring it to the notice of the Minister of Justice as of any other person.
They say their pay is very small. I understand they are getting $3.25 a day and the minister will readily understand that is very small remuneration under present conditions. They have to live in the city of Ottawa. They come from distances. They must live in respectable places and $3.25 a day has not much purchasing power at the present time. No doubt these messengers have people dependent upon them, families to support. They have been coming here for years, and they have been invited to come. I think the country should provide decently for their services, and see that they are not losing their time, and that they have something to the good when they go home for the support of those dependent upon them. I, therefoie, appeal to all the ministers here that they take the messengers' case into consideration, and out. of some vote give them such an increase in their pay as may be considered proper. Peihaps the Speaker has more to do with this class of employees than the head of any other department. The Speaker might look over the list, see what they have been receiving, and make a fair allowance to them. I happened to be addressed by some of those men, and I shall be very proud if I can be of any service to them in bringing this, matter to the notice of the House,

I desire to draw the attention of the acting Postmaster General and the Minister of Customs to an article which appeared in to-day's papers regarding the appointment of the postmaster at fvew Hamburg.
What riding is that in?

Waterloo, I think. We
have heard a great deal from the opposite side of the House regarding the treatment of returned soldiers, and I well recollect, as do other members of this committee, the vehement declaration of the Minister of Customs that returned soldiers should always be taken care of, and that they should have the first call on positions which they could fill. This appears to me to be a very striking case. A young man named Lasch-inger, who lived in New Hamburg, is about to return from the front wounded. One of his legs had to be amputated, and the index finger of his right hand is gone. His father, the postmaster at New Hamburg, died very recently and the young man, through his friends, applied for the position. It is said that 90 per cent of the inhabitants of New Hamburg signed a petition asking that this young chap be ap-

pointed. I believe he has a mother and some other members of the family -who will be practically dependent upon him. The position has not been given back to him. Instead a young man named Eau has been appointed.
A raw deal.

A raw deal and a raw
man, a wealthy man living in New Hamburg. He is very well off, and runs a local brewery, a very prosperous citizen who does not need the appointment for the purpose of a livelihood one bit. We on this side of the House have heard, without end, and without any possible end until after this election, declarations of what the Conservative party would do for the soldiers-protestations of their loyalty and so on. It has been stated. that these men would be taken care of, and that the Government party was the only people who could take care of them. Almost the first instance that happens is the case of a boy whose father had the office before him, whose family were dependent upon the revenue of that office for a livelihood, and where 90 per cent of the people of the town, including Liberals and Conservatives, signed a petition in order to have him appointed in his father's place, and we find the Government, instead of appointing that soldier boy, took the recommendation of the Conservative committee in New Hamburg and appointed a man who has always been a stalwart Conservative, who does not need the office for a livelihood and who was given that office purely on account of his party allegiance.
It would be well,"therefore, if we should hear fewer protestations of loyalty to our soldiers on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite, who seem to think that they are the only persons justified in uttering them. " By their fruits ye shall know them,"- The instance that I have quoted is a very striking one.
The hon. member has insinuated that that is the policy which is being carried out in my department.
I did not say anything of the kind.

That is the inference that I draw from his remarks. I defy the hon. gentleman to name one instance in which I have filled a position in the Customs Department by the appointment of a person other than a returned soldier.

My hon. friend admits
that the policy adopted by the Post Office Department is wrong.

The hon. member should
not put words in my mouth. I am stating the policy that I have followed in the Customs Department. So far as I know, that policy has been followed in other departments in all cases where returned soldiers have been available. The member for West Lambton has referred to the case at New Hamburg. I know nothing about it; I do not know whether or not the acting Postmaster General (Mr. Doherty) knows anything about it. My only reason for rising is to take issue with any hon. gentleman in this House who says that in the Department of 'Customs returned soldiers have not been appointed to fill vacancies. I have tried to follow out the principle of giving these positions to returned soldiers, where-ever that was possible.

Then when my hon.
friend made the declaration that returned *soldiers would be appointed, he was making it not for the Government, but simply for himself.
I stated to the hon. member that the Order in Council had been passed and that we were acting upon it.
You never observed it.
I have observed it all along; that policy has been followed out in almost every case, in accordance with the Order in Council.

When it came to the appointment of a postmaster in the town of Stellarton, the man who held the patronage was consulted, returned soldier or no returned soldier. The postmaster was dismissed, and, far from taking a returned soldier, they appointed to the position the president of the Conservative Association of that town. Further than that, they rented his store at $600 a year-a store for which no one else would pay more than $200 a year-and all this while a dozen returned soldiers were walking around the streets. The Minister of Customs is a good bluffer; he gets up and tells us what he does, and defies hon. gentlemen on the other side to do this or to do that. He is a very good fellow, but he cannot get away with that kind of thing. As to the Post Office Department, they do not pretend to observe the principle of appointing returned soldiers.

The trouble is that the hon. gentleman who is at the head of the Post Office Department is not in the House -he may be busy; I am not saying anything about that. Every week the Post Office Department violates the policy of appointing returned soldiers. The member for West Lambton mentioned a case that occurred in New Hamburg; I have in mind another case in an adjoining county. I brought it to the attention of the House some weeks ago, and a discussion thereupon arose in reference to positions in Montreal, in the course of which the Minister of Customs made certain statements. In the case to which I refer the same thing happened; the people of both political	parties	asked for
the appointment of a returned soldier who was fit for the	position, but the
recommendation of the member for the district was acted upon and .the position was given to a politician, just as if no policy had been adopted of appointing returned soldiers. Moreover, that action was contrary to the wishes of the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When and where did
that happen?

I will look it up in
Hansard. It was in a western Ontario constituency; the member for the district was in the House when I made the statement, and he offered no contradiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When was it?

About two weeks ago; I cannot tell the exact date. We had a general discussion then about the appointment of returned soldiers, which, I think, led up to the announcement that was made by the Minister of Customs.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend will admit that that information is somewhat vague. If positive statements are made and I am held responsible, 1 should be informed when and where the instances have occurred.
Mr. GRAiHAM:	I will look up the details and let my hon. friend know. It is in Hansard; I thought that after the discussion that took place every one would be familiar with the circumstances of the case. If the hon. gentleman was not. in the House, I should have thought that he would be informed by other ministers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Unfortunately, things
go on Hansard that are the result of misinformation on the part of gentlemen who may make statements in good faith. As a matter of fairness, when we are told that
these things are being done every week, we should be informed also when and where they have occurred.

What about the
Stellarton case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When did the Stellarton case occur?	-
About four months ago. I brought the matter up twice; my hon. friend ought to have looked into it before now.
Pleading ignorance is a poor excuse.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A question was put about a building that had been rented for the Stellarton post office. I certainly have no recollection of the hon. gentleman's making any statement, when I was present, concerning the matter to which he refers.

I put another question on the Order Paper in regard to the dismissal of the postmaster and the appointment of another person to the position. Possibly my hon. friend (Mr. Doherty) was not acting minister at that time. Anyway, the answer was put on Hansard. I can cite another instance, the case of the vacancy in the postmastership at Charlottetown. The people in the city were pressing for the appointment of a very prominent returned soldier, but their representations were disregarded; the recommendation of the members for the county was accepted and another man appointed.

Another case came to my
attention some time ago. A young man who had been employed as a messenger in this House returned from the front with one of his arms disabled as a result of injuries received in the firing line. He told me that he had been recommended for a position in the Department of Naval Affairs at a salary of $90 a month. After working there for some two weeks, he was dismissed and a young lady was given his position. He was then given employment as a messenger in this building-he is not here at present, so anything that I may say will not prejudice him in any employment that he would receive from a department of the Government. I think it is wed that we should do what we can to remove the masks which hon. gentlemen sitting on the treasury benches are wearing so smugly in this matter. Only a few months ago it was stated in the Toronto papers that a returned soldier who applied for a position was told to go to the chairman of the Conservative Patronage Committee. There



has been no denial of that. Hon. gentlemen who are interested may profess great indignation, but everybody knows throughout the country that the only use the Government has for returned soldiers is the use that they make of them at election time. In my constituency there are a number of returned soldiers. Two positions have been vacant during the last four years-preventive officer of Customs and collector of Customs. These vacancies are not filled because the dispenser of political patronage in my constituency has promised the position to so many that he dare not fill it until the election is over- and then it will be too late. Why are returned soldiers in my constituency not appointed to those positions? Because, as I say, the political patronage managers insist that these appointments shall go not to men who have won glory and performed service on the battlefield, but to men who are performing service for the Conservative party in the constituency in which they reside.

I understood the Minister of Customs to say that by Order in Council the Government had determined upon a policy of giving preference to returned soldiers. As forewarned is forearmed, I want to draw the attention of the acting Postmaster General ito the fact that tenders are being asked for a mail route running out of Hem-mingford. One of the tenderers is a returned soldier who was wounded. I met him yesterday at a local fair. He told me he had put in his tender, and had attached to his tender the certificate from the doctor certifying to his injury. Will the minister now say, that, all conditions being equal, he will give the preference to this returned soldier?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If all conditions are equal I certainly would carry out the provision of the Order in Council. Hon. gentlemen have spoken very loudly and violently and have told us about what "everybody" knew. They have been very vague-in particular the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte). They have covered a very wide field. I do not quite see that that is a fair method to prove a charge. If the policy has been departed from in the Post Office Department it is most assuredly not within my knowledge. It is not quite conclusive to say: There is a position; there is a returned soldier; the returned soldier, and the position do not come in contact; therefore, you are departing from your system. Hon. gentlemen, I suppose, will admit there

are certain classes of men with certain qualifications suited to fill certain positions, and I do not suppose that the suggestion is that the mere fact of a man being a returned soldier, and the mere fact of there existing a vacant position without regard to the qualifications of the returned soldier on the one side and the requirements of the position on the other, should cause the position at once to he filled by the returned soldier. The hon. gentleman puts to me the question in a perfectly fair way. Other things being equal, the provision of the Order in Council would call for preference being given to the returned soldier. I do not think hon. gentlemen will show that, in my personal action, that being the condition, the Order in Council has not been acted upon.

I will recall to the Acting Postmaster General a case in which, perhaps, he will admit that the returned soldier was qualified. Take the case of the post office in the city of Charlottetown, P.E.I. A vacancy occurred there some time ago. A returned soldier, who was a university graduate, was an applicant for the position. He was recommended by most of the responsible people in the city of Charlottetown, hut he did not receive the appointment. Political considerations again intervened, and the position went to the man who had the recommendation of the patronage committee. There is clearly a ease in which the applicant, a returned soldier, came in contact with the position, and had all the qualifications necessary, but he did not receive the appointment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman's position that every university graduate is the best man to be appointed to fill a position in a post office in any particular place?

I should think, if a university graduate is available for the position of postmaster in Charlottetown, the acting Postmaster General would have to furnish pretty good evidence to the contrary before he could convince anybody that that man was not competent to take charge of it. I do not wish to hold the acting Postmaster General responsible for this. I am speaking generally in regard to the Government. The policy the Government has laid down in Orders in Council, which have been, flaunted frequently before the faces of hon. members on this side of the House, is being violated every day, and the acting Postmaster General, as a member of the Government, must take his full share of responsibility in the matter.

If the statements made by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) are true, what does the minister purpose doing about the Charlottetown case? Will he give the position to the university graduate who is a wounded soldier and who has returned?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will make inquiry as to the qualifications of the respective candidates. I have the honour to be a university graduate myself, and I am prepared to concede that there are hundreds of men who are not university graduates who are more competent to fill the position of postmaster almost anywhere than I should be. I cannot accept the test of being a university graduate as a proof of competence to fill the position.
There is only one test-the political test.
You ought to call in the Civil Service Act.

The Government ought to admit that all these appointments are made on the recommendation of the patronage committee. Those patronage committees are just as active in all the constituencies throughout the country as they were before the war broke out. Patronage is everywhere. The other day a gentleman in Montreal to whom a young lady, a nurse, applied for a recommendation, saying she wanted to serve her country, said to her: "I shall be very glad to come to Ottawa and see what I can do for you." This is the statement of a man of the very highest character. When he came to Ottawa he was asked what this young lady's father - was in politics.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: By whom?
By somebody in Ottawa to whom he went.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Somebody!
Oh, oh.

A gentleman to whom he thought he ought to go in order to get the position for this lady. I know of another case in which a medical man in charge of an ambulance corps was urged' by a prominent member of the patronage committee to take on some nurses. He declined because he did not want them. He was called up again and asked if he was not going to play the game fairly. He declined again. It was not long before, I am told, a peremptory order came from Ottawa to take on one of those nurses at once, although there was
3S3i
absolutely no reason in the world why she should be taken on, because her services were not required. In the city of St. John, from which I come, it is known by everybody that since the war began the patronage committee is the Government so far as that constituency is concerned. I believe that is the case also throughout the country. You may speak about the affairs of Canada being administered from Ottawa, they are not; they are administered by the patronage committees in the different constituencies. The patronage committees form a part of the machinery of this Government. Not long ago, there was a proposition to form a Union Government, and it was suggested that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) should be the Prime Minister of this country. At a caucus of my hon. friends opposite, they stated they would not have the Minister of Trade and Commerce as Prime Minister. They knew that he had declared in this House that he was opposed to patronage, and they considered that if he became Prime Minister patronage would be done away with. Tnere-fore they refused to entertain the suggestion that he should become Prime Minister. The party machine must still continue, as under Union Government the Conservative party machine would continue to administer the affairs of this Dominion from coast to coast.
With regard to my hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee), who spoke of the very great hardship to this boy and his family by reason of his not being allowed to have the position for which he was recommended and which his father had previously filled, I suppose he has been informed that his female relatives are to be allowed to vote in the next election. Why, then, should they complain? Surely that ought to be a compensation for any financial distress which they may suffer. Has my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Weichel) written to them that they are to be allowed to vote in the coming election, and therefore they must not complain that their brother is ill-treated in respect to the position?
In Military District No. 6, in the Maritime Provinces, to-day there are 257 gentlemen bolding positions in the Militia Department, only ten of whom have been overseas, while there are in the Great War Veterans' Association of St. John, I think about 350 members, who could easily be placed in those positions, running from small salaries up to the enormous sum of

$6,200 per year. Let ime read the resolution which the Great War Veterans' Association have sent me, and I do it because it shows that it is all a holloiw pretense to say that this Government is prepared to do everything it can for the returned soldier. The resolution, which was passed at a general meeting at St. John on September 12, 1917, is as follows:
