Resolved, that the attention of the Premier and Minister of Militia and Defence be drawn to the state of affairs existing in the Militia Department, District No. 6. In a recent list of officers employed in Military District No. 6, there was shown to he 257 holding positions, of whom only 10 had seen service at the front, and these were all holding minor positions, while the better positions were held by officers who had never seen service overseas or had made no attempt to do so.
Therefore, resolved that these officers should be made to go overseas or revert to civil life and take their chance with conscripts when called, and their places taken by returned officers who have done their duty for the Umpire.
Also that ail men employed in safety-first jobs who have not been overseas be sent immediately to the front and their places taken with returned men wounded for their country.
Further resolved that a copy of this resolution be sent to Hon. J. D. Hazen and Hon. Dr. Pugsley as minister and members of St. John, and they be asked to take a definite stand in this matter and report same and advise the Intention of the Government in this matter.
Tours respectfully,
(Sgd.) E. J. Puddy, Secretary, The Great War Veterans' Association, St. John.
I bring this before the House and, through Hansard, before the people of this country. I say that these returned soldiers are realizing to-day that they are not receiving fair treatment at the hands of this Government, and it is necessary the Government should be aroused to a sense of its duty in . respect of positions which returned soldiers could fill. They are now walking the streets, waiting for recognition, feeling that their services demand recognition, hut as I	have	said,	all	the	recognitionwhich	they	.are	to	get	from this
Government practically is that their female relatives are to he allowed 'to vote. Why should they not complain at this treatment? Is the mere privilege of voting to be regarded by this Government as being a fair and reasonable recognition of the services which these men have performed for their country?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I suppose hon. gentlemen opposite consider it a fitting opportunity to make vague charges of insincerity against the Government with respect to returned soldiers now, just as the session is to close, and when in all probability no

individual case, if the hon. member has courage enough to mention any case, can be investigated closely and replied to fully. We are charged with extreme partisanship, running the country by patronage committees-charged by hon. gentlemen opposite who, throughout this session, have displayed a partisanship that should make them historic and immortal. This session has witnessed an effort on the part of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, concurred in by the whole party, to bury partisanship so far as the war is concerned, and to share the Government of Canada with all who are in favour of this war-an offer declined by hon. gentlemen opposite who raised the flag of party, fought under the flag of party, and persisted in fighting under the flag of party to the end.
A case was mentioned by the hon. member for West Lambtom (Mr. Pardee) as taking place in the town of New Hamburg, I know the town of New Hamburg, but I never heard of this case. The member for the county is absent to-day, but I know that he intends to contest that constituency at the next election, and I know he would not make any mistake in the town of New Hamburg in regard to returned soldiers. I think he may be able to speak to the case to-morrow, and I hope he will be able to do so. The facts are not all brought out with regard to that case yet. To say that 90 per cent of the town of New Hamburg supported this returned soldier for postmaster and that he was refused the appointment is not a full statement of the case, even if it is correct so far as it goes, and I question very much if the information of the hon. member for West Lambton is correct. To lay down the proposition that because a man is a university graduate, all other considerations as to qualifications must be laid aside, and that that fact alone establishes that he should have the appointment, is a very strange proposition for a member of this Parliament to lay down. Do hon. gentlemen not know university graduates who are about the least well qualified people they could think of for the position of postmaster? I know nothing of the case in the city of Charlottetown, but the city of Charlottetown will pass on that case when it comes to the contest at the polls. I venture to say that when charges are made in the city of Charlottetown about returned soldiers being treated unjustly the charges will have reference to the western coast. It will be a case of the hon. member for St. John over again: somebody told somebody else in some far-off city that somebody could not get a position unless her father

voted so and so, or some one told some one else in the city of Toronto that he had to go to the Patronage Committee to get the position. These *will be the charges levelled in Charlottetown, instead of bringing up an individual case in that city where the facts would be well known. I think it is altogether unlikely that an injustice would be done in that city any more than anywhere else.
I am engaged at the present time in correspondence with a returned soldier from the western provinces. He is a man with a family, but he left his family and went overseas. He left a Government job, not under a Conservative Government, but under a Liberal Government, and he is still pleading to get the job back which he left.
Under what Government?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The Government of
Manitoba.
They are for union Government.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Not being able to get h's job back, he appeals to the Government of Canada to provide something for him.
What was his name and position?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I will not give his name.
It is you who are now making vague charges.
Is it Doctor Simpson?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
When I have a charge to make against hon. gentlemen opposite, I will name the man. I do not want to do an injustice to him, or to prejudice his chances of getting that position. It would be unjust to him to mention his name; the hon. gentleman knows that. But those are the facts just the same. I do not say that there is no reason why he should not get his position back. There may be a reason I know nothing of, but if there is such, I know not what it is. It just shows that one needs to know all the facts of a case before making charges against any one. There are returned soldiers in every province. There are perhaps returned soldiers who have not Government positions, but for the most part, they have all some sort of position out in the province from whicu I come. Not only in cases where tne merits are about even, but where they are anything like even, the position in all cases I ever heard of, goes to the returned soldier. Many and many a position in the province
of Manitoba has gone to a returned soldier, and nobody has ever complained about a Patronage Committee that I ever heard of. For that matter, I have no Patronage Committee.
I know not in the province of Manitoba of a single complaint that any returned soldier has been done an injustice. There are positions that all returned soldiers cannot fill. There are very few positions that all returned soliders can fill. And it does not do a returned soldier any good to put him in a position he is not qualified to fill. A returned soldier cannot fill many a staff position and you give hi,m no advantage by placing him in a position he is unfitted for. Instead of doing him a benefit, you do him an injury. I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite to point to an individual case, and if they can establish it against us then they have gone a lot further than they have gone to-night. Wherever that case is it will be under review in the constituency when we come to the polls, and I have no doubt whatever how the returned soldiers of this country are going to vote, and the result.

Would you like to bet
on it?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
That is always the answer of the man who has no other answer " would you like to bet?"
Mr. PUiGSLEY: Don't foe too confident.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Let hon. gentlemen
bring up the treatment of returned soldiers, not in constituencies a thousand miles away on the word of somebody, or nobody, or everybody, but let them bring it up in the very constituency itself, and thresh it out on its merits, and the people will give their verdict, and we have no fear of if.

It is not altogether fair for the Secretary of State to charge hon. members on this side of the House with being indefinite in-their criticism. I think they have been very definite. My hon. friend from West Lamfoton (Mr. Pardee) has given him a specific case, which he has not been able to answer. My hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) has given him another specific case, well known in eastern Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. He has made no reply. My hon. friend from Pictou (M;. Macdonald) has mentioned another case ;n the town of Stellarton. The Secretary of State has not been able to answer any of these. If he wants another case, I will give him a fourth.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The case in Stellarton was four months ago, when the acting minister was not in charge of the office. Why did not the hon. memtber put a question on the Order Paper and bring the matter up then?
The question was on the Order Paper long ago.

The case I have in mind is that of a returned nurse. Recently the Government established a hospital in the city of Sydney, called the Moxham Hospital for convalescent soldiers. It was necessary to engage a matron to take charge of the hospital. A very competent young lady, who had seen service at the front, made application for the position. Every one said she was well qualified and should have been appointed. Her name is Miss Black, and the Secretary of State can make investigation about this and see if the facts as I present them are correct.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Is that the military hospital?
Mr. SINCLAIR- Yes. This young lady was not acceptable to the patronage committee of South Cape Breton.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Is it under the Military Hospitals Commission?

I suppose so. In any event, she was not acceptable to the patronage committee of South Cape Breton, and her application was rejected, the position being given to a young lady who had no experience at all, but who had simply completed her training as ia nurse, but her father was a friend of the party in power. This case is well known in the county of Cape Breton. I think we should have no trouble in giving my hon. friend a great many other cases of a similar nature. My experience in regard to the cases of any of the nurses I have been acquainted with is that they got on the force only through the recommendation of some Conservative politician, and I can give the minister specific instances of nurses making application to be put on the service whose applications lay for months in the military head office here, and there was nothing doing until they secured the recommendation of some prominent Tory supporter . That has been the system of the appointment of nurses all through the service. I do not want to bother the Secretary of State by giving him too many specific cases, but it is not fair for him to say that members on this side of the House are making general charges only, when, as

a matter of fact, we have been giving him specific cases which he has not been able to explain.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have had the explanation of one of the cases already. Perhaps it is as well to give it to the committee. I have not had time to communicate it to the acting Postmaster General. The hon. member for Prince Edward Island (Mr. McLean) tells me that what the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) says as to Charlottetown is quite wrong, that there has been no appointment made at all to the position of postmaster at Charlottetown, that the inspector who was inspector before is doing the work along with his own work, and saving the country $2,000 a year.

He will be in the estimates for extra work done. This condition of affairs will only last until after the election.
Progress reported.
The House proceeded to consider resolutions reported from Committee of Supply.

I do not think it necessary to read ,all these items, but I would like to speak of one matter. There is an item for improvement work in St. John harbour, and I wish to call the attention of the Acting Minister of Public., Works to what I think is a very serious state of affairs in connection with this work. There was a contract given for a large amount of work there, including the building of a dry dock. When I was minister, I exacted a security of half a million dollars. I am told that the Government has reduced the security to $250,000, and that drawbacks accumulated, and that the contractors were at work and had a large plant on the spot, worth $300,000 or $400,000, in respect of which the department would have a lien for the purpose of the work. There was also about $700,000 of cash on hand including the deposit. I understand the Government has returned to the contractors the whole $700,000, and that the contractors are now trying to get the plant released. If that is done, it will he handing over to defaulting contractors, who were under obligation to perform this work, nearly $1,000,000 which this country had a right to insist should be applied towards the completion of the work. I do not think my hon. friend is responsible, but the Government is responsible, and I would ask him to exercise the right of lien which the Government has on that plant to keep it

there until matters can be arranged for the completion of the work.
I am not going to criticise to-night anything in connection with the half million dollars; perhaps that can be satisfactorily explained. But I would ask the minister to retain control of the plant until satisfactory arrangements are made for the continuance of the work and the unravelling of all matters connected with the dry dock.

The amount that was handed to the Government went to pay the creditors. With reference to the plant, I promise my hon. friend that I will take it up in the morning .with the officials of the department, see what the situation is and if it is as the hon. member states we will hold it back.

If my hon. friend will look at the contract he will see that the Government has a lien on all plant brought to the work.
Resolution concurred in.

I suppose that the Government will see that all these items are right. When we dispense with reading them the Government will have to take the responsibility of seeing that the details are correct.
Resolution concurred in.

On motion of Mr. Reid, the House went into committee of Ways and Means, Mr. Rainville in the chair.

Resolved, that towards making good the supply granted to His Majesty on account of certain expenditures of the public service for the financial year ending March 31, 1918, the sum of $4,721,500 be granted out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
Motion agreed to.
Mr. Reid moved:
Resolved, that towards making good the supply granted to His Majesty on aooount of certain expenditures of the public service for the financial year ending March 31, 1918, the sum of $46,375,267.75 be granted out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
Motion agreed to.
Resolutions reported and concurred in.

Mr. Reid moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 135, for granting to His Majesty certain sums of money for the public service for the financial year ending the 31st March, 1918.
Motion agreed to, Ball read the first and second time, considered in committee, and reported.
On the motion for the third reading of the Bill:

["An Act of this kind was found to be absolutely necessary in England even after a few months of war. The general public were willing to give generously, but they were very susceptible, the result being that they were easily exploited. We had the same experience in Canada. One of the things that must be conserved in this war, quite as much as provisions or money, is the generous impulse of our people. We must not allow them to be exploited, because there is only a certain amount of voluntary generous impulse in the country. If that is drawn off and misused, there is so much less for legitimate enterprise. I can give to this House any number of instances that have come within the experience of the Canadian Patriotic Fund, in which we have seen the well-intentioned generosity of the Canadian people deliberately diverted and wasted on war funds. This Bill has a double purpose. First of all, it purposes protecting the public against fraudulent, unwise, injudicious collection of money for so-called war charities, and, secondly, we want it very much in order to protect the legitimate funds, to make it possible for the legitimate funds to defend themselves.
The National Canadian Patriotic Fund will be one of the first to ask to be registered. It will !be the easiest thing in the world for that fund to conform with all the regulations that are required. They have to prove that they are administered by a responsible committee; that they keep regular minutes of their meetings; that they have proper books, and that their income and outgo are properly checked. They have to show that they bank their money, and that they use the authorized forms of the department. The National Canadian Patriotic Fund, the Belgian Fund, and the Red Cross Fund, through their organizations, will come and 'be certificated. Their certificates will apply not only to the national fund, but to all the branches. Each of the branches m its respective locality has, to some extent, the same powers that the parent organization has, and what will happen will be just this: If a city organization undertakes to raise money for the Patriotic Fund they will have to Obtain permission from the local branch in order to do so. The local branch can say to those people: That is not the proper way in which to go to work for the Patriotic Fund; a large percentage of the amount

collected will foe wasted. We had in Vancouver a case in which they got up a large contribution contrary to the desire of the local branch of the Patriotic Fund. They raised $1,500 and paid out $1,400 in expenses. That, was a pure waste of benevolent efforT. The various funds of this country are entitled to protect themselves against misdirected effort.
Bill as amended reported, amendments read the first and second time and concurred in, and Bill read the third time and passed.
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Reid, the House adjourned at 1.40 a.m. Thursday.
Thursday, September 20, 1917."]

Unless there is some special reason that the Government can give us why this Bill should be read a third time to-night, it should not be read a third time. I do not want to take any objection, but to go through the first, second and third reading without taking a breath is rushing matters somewhat unless there is some special reason for it.

We would like to pass it tonight to get it over to the Senate. I understand the Senate is practically through. They have passed the War-time Elections Bill and it will be here to-night.
We would like to send over to the Senate what we have on the Order Paper, so that they may have some business to-morrow. When we get through with the Bill which is coming over, we will have nothing more to do. We would like to take it up, discuss it, and be ready for prorogation to-morrow. If, by any chance, we cannot get through with the discussion, prorogation will take place the next day, but we would like to get our Bills over there in order to finish up the business.

Of course, there will be some discussion on the other Bill I imagine, but before I consent to the third reading I would ask if the War-time Elections Act is back from the Senate and is to be dealt with to-night. It cannot be discussed tomorrow, unless steps are taken to-night so that it will appear on the Order Paper. Otherwise, the discussion will take place the day after to-morrow.

The Bill I refer to has
passed the Senate, and, as I understand, was sent over here, and will be ready for-to-morrow. At all events, we would like to finish up the other business and be prepared to discuss the War-time Elections Act to-morrow. I understand that the Senate came to some arrangement by which the Bill passed there without further discussion. I admit there will be some discussion here. I have no doubt the Bill will be ready for discussion to-morrow.

If I might be permitted, under the rules the Bill cannot be here for discussion at the next sitting, unless it goes through the proper stages, and is sent over

to us to-night. If it is presented to the House to-night, it will he on the Order Paper to be discussed to-morrow.
I have information that the Bill will be here inside of ten minutes, so it will be on the Order Paper to-morrow; that will be arranged.

Might I suggest that
the amendments should be printed, as they refer to my province. They are very intricate, and I would like to see them.
Yes, they will be printed.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the third time.
The House proceeded to the consideration of an amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. 66 to amend the Judges' Act.
I suggest that this debate be under closure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understood that this stood over, in order that the formal motion might properly be submitted to the House.
I move:
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their honours that this House disagrees to their amendment to Bill No. 66 an Act to amend the Judges' Act, for the following reasons:
Because the amendment is not relevant to the Bill, which is only to provide the salaries for two additional fudges, to restrict in certain cases the travelling expenses of judges and to extend certain provisions of the Act now applying to County Court judges to the Circuit Court of the district of Montreal;
Because, though it may be advisable to modify the pensions at present provided with respect to future appointments, it is not in the public interests that the remuneration or pensions of judges now on the Bench should be changed to their prejudice;
Because, the amendment forbids the judges to perform any duties outside their judicial duties, and that, while it may be an advantage to make more precise and definite the prohibitions at present existing, there are duties that every one is bound to perform, that so wide a prohibition is impossible for the judges to observe, and that, in any case, it is not in the public interest to enforce so unlimited a restriction.
Because there are in connection with said amendment questions of grave importance touching the independence of the judiciary, which call for the careful consideration of the House of Commons, consideration which cannot adequately be given at the present session, and because these questions can be more advantageously dealt with upon a Bill submitted for that purpose, and at a time when they can be deliberately considered.
What will be the result if this motion is adopted? Where does the Bill go then?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It will be returned to the Senate. While I have no official information on the .subject, I believe there is very good reason: to believe that they will .acquiesce in the soundness of these reasons, which only look to defer consideration of the important questions which arise on their amendment, which is entirely foreign to anything in the Bill.
The Bill will get through? Mr. DOHERTY: Yes.
House again in committee on Bill No. 130, relating to war charities, Mr. Rainville in the Chair.
Is that the Act to provide for the supervision of the collection of war charges?
Yes.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The 'Minister of Finance is confined to his room. Consequently, I made as good a study of the measure this afternoon as I could, and I read the whole debate that took place on the measure when it was in committee before. I think my hon. friend is wrong when he says there was information to come. I cannot reeol-leot that.
He held it over for some reason.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I know the reason; it was not for information. There were certain suggested amendments. It was suggested that it should be amended in three ways. First objection was taken to the title. The hon. member for Piotou (Mr. Macdonald) thought the title should be "The War Contributions Act." Secondly, the hon. member for Pictou thought it should be widened to include such contributions as machine gun contributions and the like of that, that it should he extended beyond the mere domain of benevolence. Thirdly, it was contended by the hon. member for Middlesex, and several hon. gentlemen opposite, that churches should be exempted from the operation of the Act.
I do not know of any other amendment that was suggested. That was why it was

held over, and consideration was promised to those suggestions. I would prefer to see the title stay as it is. The title "War Contributions" would not definitely indicate the nature of the Bill. It is a Bill to prevent people appealing to the public for money for an unauthorized fund, or a fund which it is not in the public interest that appeals should be made for. It does not cover the whole scope of war contribution. It covers only benevolent or alleged benovelent contributions, or charitable contributions, because there is really nothing distasteful in the word "charity."
The title to be given to this Act is the same as that which has been given to the British Act; their War Charities Act is in line with this legislation. They have had their legislation since the war began; in my judgment, we should have had this sooner. The member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) suggested long ago that some such legislation as this should be provided. We are following in line with Britain in that regard; besides, the title "War Charities" is appropriate. As to the other idea that the Bill should cover a wider sphere, it may be that we ought to do that in separate legislation, but anything done in that regard should not be done in connection with this measure. The things we want to aim at now are appeals to the charity of the public and to the benevolence of the public for the relieving of suffering and distress. The other various schemes that were worked- some of them very laudable indeed in themselves-are now pretty much in the past;
1	do not think that we need look for them much more. The suggestion of hon. gentlemen opposite that churches should be excepted, is a good one. I move that section
2	be amended by adding after the word " association " in the second line the words "other than a church or the Salvation Army."
Amendment agreed to.

There was a discussion as
to the desirability of exempting an organization of a national character, such as the Daughters of the Empire. Possibly, however, if you started on one you would have to introduce quite a number of exemptions of this kind.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I do not see any need of exemptions. I do not take quite the same view of the operation of the Act as that taken by the 'Minister of Finance. He seemed to proceed on the assumption that any institutions that were obviously
and by general acceptance right and proper and already recognized by law should be exempted. My idea is that they should be immediately registered. The Secretary of State has power to register them at once, and my first step would be to register the Daughters of the Empire, the Patriotic Fund, the Red Cross, the Belgian Relief Fund, and the like. These organizations will lead in the matter of registration.

I understand that this Bill enables the minister to frant licenses for the holding of entertainments at which moneys -will be collected for patriotic purposes, and that if such licenses are not issued, those responsible for the entertainment will be acting in violation of the law. I do not think that we have any jurisdiction to grant licenses for entertainments held in any of the provinces.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not think that my hon. friend has in his mind quite the right idea of the nature of the Bill. In the first place, we do not grant licenses. We register the fund, which is the institution that embodies the purpose of the appeal. For example, we register the Patriotic Fund; that does not mean that we license a church or a society in the country to hold a concert on behalf of the Patriotic Fund. Contributions to that fund by way of concert or entertainment are all right provided the Patriotic Fund themselves say that they are prepared to accept the contribution and that the concert or entertainment has their sanction. But we want to stop the carrying out of schemes, even in respect of the Patriotic Fund, the purpose of which is ostensibly to obtain money for the Patriotic Fund, but really to get money which goes largely to the promoters of the schemes or their friends, the Patriotic Fund getting only a negligible residue.

No form of criminal ingenuity could be practised in connection with getting funds that is not a violation of the provisions of the Criminal Code. If it is stated that money received or collected will be given to one purpose and it is deliberately given to another, money is received on false pretenses. If funds are misappropriated, the persons responsible are guilty of conversion and of theft. I do not see that anything a man or woman could do in exploiting schemes of this kind in a criminal way is not covered by the provisions of the criminal law. I think that this proposed1 Act is an absolutely unnecessary provision.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The criminal law does not cover the cases dealt with here, so far as they have been presented to me. For example, it was advertised that at a race meeting the proceeds of the first day should go to the Patriotic Fund. As a consequence patriotically inclined people went on the first day in preference to the other days, and many who went, instead of asking for change, left their five dollars with the gatekeeper. They thought that it was all going to the Patrigtic Fund; that was all they cared about it. As a consequence some $6,000 or $7,000 were taken in that day. Some difficulty ensued in getting the money; much time was taken up, and finally about $350 reached the Patriotic Fund. The rest was applied towards the expenses of the meeting, salaries and allowances to those who gave their time to it, and so on. That would not come under the Criminal Code, but no such scheme of making money for the Patriotic Fund-it was really not for the fund at all-should be allowed. It is such things as that that we want to regulate by this Bill. The secretary of the Patriotic Fund can give my hon. friend some very illuminating instances.

Suppose it was advertised that the funds were to be applied to the Patriotic Fund and that the people in the light of that advertisement, went and contributed their money. That money would have been received illegally, under false pretenses, if it was not afterwards handed over to the Patriotic Fund.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The proceeds were applied to the Patriotic Fund all right, but the promoters took care that the proceeds did not amount to very much.

I remember the argument of the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) on that point when this matter was before the House on a previous occasion. I believe that even if the Criminal Code does provide punishment for fraudulent collection of funds of this kind, yet in these times it is a great deterrent and discouragement to funds supported by voluntary contribution if those frauds are allowed to go to a point at which action has to be taken which may ultimately result in a prosecution. The old 'adage that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure very fitly applies to a matter of this kind, and it ought to he checked by prevention rather than by punishment after frauds have been perpetrated. For that reason I can conceive that an Act along the lines of the one before the House will more effectively meet

the case than by resorting to punishment after the wrong has been done.

An Act of this kind was found to be absolutely necessary in England even after a few months of war. The general public were willing to give generously, but they were very susceptible, the result being that they were easily exploited. We had the same experience in Canada. One of the things that must be conserved in this war, quite as much as provisions or money, is the generous impulse of our people. We must not allow them to be exploited, because there is only a certain amount of voluntary generous impulse in the country. If that is drawn off and misused, there is so much less for legitimate enterprise. I can give to this House any number of instances that have come within the experience of the Canadian Patriotic Fund, in which we have seen the well-intentioned generosity of the Canadian people deliberately diverted and wasted on war funds. This Bill has a double purpose. First of all, it purposes protecting the public against fraudulent, unwise, injudicious collection of money for so-called war charities, and, secondly, we want it very much in order to protect the legitimate funds, to make it possible for the legitimate funds to defend themselves.
The National Canadian Patriotic Fund will be one of the first to ask to be registered. It will !be the easiest thing in the world for that fund to conform with all the regulations that are required. They have to prove that they are administered by a responsible committee; that they keep regular minutes of their meetings; that they have proper books, and that their income and outgo are properly checked. They have to show that they bank their money, and that they use the authorized forms of the department. The National Canadian Patriotic Fund, the Belgian Fund, and the Red Cross Fund, through their organizations, will come and 'be certificated. Their certificates will apply not only to the national fund, but to all the branches. Each of the branches m its respective locality has, to some extent, the same powers that the parent organization has, and what will happen will be just this: If a city organization undertakes to raise money for the Patriotic Fund they will have to Obtain permission from the local branch in order to do so. The local branch can say to those people: That is not the proper way in which to go to work for the Patriotic Fund; a large percentage of the amount

collected will foe wasted. We had in Vancouver a case in which they got up a large contribution contrary to the desire of the local branch of the Patriotic Fund. They raised $1,500 and paid out $1,400 in expenses. That, was a pure waste of benevolent efforT. The various funds of this country are entitled to protect themselves against misdirected effort.
Bill as amended reported, amendments read the first and second time and concurred in, and Bill read the third time and passed.
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Reid, the House adjourned at 1.40 a.m. Thursday.
Thursday, September 20, 1917.
